meta.title: Pre-Islamic Arabia: a mapped chronology, 300–640 CE
meta.note: Hand-built timeline and gazetteer for an interactive historical map, graded entry by entry: EPI is inscription-fixed, EXT is an external Greek/Syriac/Latin/Persian source, TRAD is later Arabic-Islamic tradition, RECON is modern scholarly reconstruction. Dates in the Arabian interior are almost all back-calculations, and the certainty fields say which. Every event also carries dateNote, one sentence on what the date actually rests on, and the boolean estimated: true where the year is a convention or a midpoint rather than a transmitted date, so an interface should render it as 'c. 570'. dateRange is the honest spread and endYear is set where the span itself is the event. The revision of 2026-10-19 also applied corrections from the Arabic-language sources where they contradict the English reconstruction this file was first built on; REVISION.ar.md lists them entry by entry, and arabia.ar.json carries the Arabic text of every record.

places.name: al-Ḥīra
places.blurb: The Lakhmid capital on the desert edge, about 7 km east-south-east of Najaf, near present-day Kūfa and close to the Euphrates, with a branch of the river reaching it. The Arabic sources date the oldest documented mention of the place to 132 CE, when Palmyrene forces were stationed there — two centuries before the Lakhm shaykhs. A Christian Arab city of palaces, monasteries and salaried scribes, with Persian-language administration, a local Hīrī script that fed into Arabic, and children from the nearby villages sent in to learn writing. It killed three of its own poets in forty-five years.

places.name: al-Khawarnaq
places.blurb: The most famous Lakhmid building, near al-Ḥīra, said to have been put up by al-Nuʿmān I to house the Sasanian prince Bahrām V, and its Roman architect Sinimmār said to have been killed so he could not build its like anywhere else. Al-Nuʿmān III received the poets of the Arabs here and held a literary session in it called al-Muʾtamar; the palace kept craftsmen on, and a line of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm is cited for it. Unlocated.

places.name: Ctesiphon / al-Madāʾin
places.blurb: The Sasanian capital on the Tigris, where Arab client kings came to petition, where ʿAdī ibn Zayd was schooled, and where the True Cross was carried in 614. Al-Nuʿmān III was seized here in 602.

places.name: Khānaqīn
places.blurb: A Zagros-foothill town where Khusraw II imprisoned the last Lakhmid king after deposing him. Al-Nuʿmān III is said to have died here of plague.

places.name: al-Nahrawān
places.blurb: Canal country east of Ctesiphon where al-Nuʿmān III fought beside the fugitive Khusraw II against the usurper Bahrām Chōbīn.

places.name: Dhū Qār
places.blurb: The watering place where Bakr ibn Wāʾil beat a Sasanian column. Where it was is genuinely disputed: the Arabic sources put it at Ṭarīf, south of Medina in the north of the peninsula, while the usual placement in southern Iraq west of the Euphrates is an inference from the name of the modern Iraqi governorate. No source identifies the site. The coordinates here follow the common Iraqi placement and should be read as a guess with a rival candidate a thousand kilometres away.

places.name: Constantinople
places.blurb: The imperial city at the far end of the road from al-Ḥīra. Imruʾ al-Qays went there to beg troops from Justinian; ʿAdī ibn Zayd went in 579 as a Sasanian envoy and came back with books.

places.name: Ankara
places.blurb: Anatolian city where Imruʾ al-Qays fell ill and died on the road home. A tomb at Hıdırlık is traditionally pointed out as his.

places.name: Chalcis / Qinnasrīn
places.blurb: A fortified town south-west of Aleppo, now identified as the field of Yawm Ḥalīma in June 554, where the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III was killed.

places.name: Ruṣāfa / Sergiopolis
places.blurb: The great desert shrine of St Sergius, patron of Arab Christians, with basilicas and a building commissioned by the Ghassanid al-Mundhir. Byzantium and the Ghassanids were reconciled here in 575.

places.name: Zabad
places.blurb: A village south-east of Aleppo whose martyrium of St Sergius carries the earliest dated Paleo-Arabic inscription, trilingual in Greek, Syriac and Arabic, from 512.

places.name: Callinicum / al-Raqqa
places.blurb: Euphrates crossing where Belisarius was beaten in 531 by Persians and Lakhmids, and where two Greek sources flatly contradict each other about whether the Ghassanid Arabs ran or held.

places.name: Thannuris
places.blurb: Mesopotamian battlefield of 528 where the Ghassanid king Jabalah IV was killed fighting for Byzantium.

places.name: Dara
places.blurb: The fortress Anastasius built against Persian Nisibis from 505, lost to Khusraw I in 573 and handed back in 591. The hinge of the whole northern frontier.

places.name: Antioch
places.blurb: The great city of Roman Syria, which al-Mundhir III raided up to but never took, and which the Persians looted in 613.

places.name: Damascus
places.blurb: Northern terminus of the Quraysh summer caravans and the city the Ghassanid camps sat behind. Fell to the Persians in 613.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.blurb: Taken by the Persians in 614 after a three-week siege; the True Cross was carried off to Ctesiphon, a loss the whole Christian East felt.

places.name: Alexandria
places.blurb: Egypt's port and grain engine, which fell to the Persians after a year-long siege in 618 — after which the Constantinople bread dole was abolished.

places.name: Bosra
places.blurb: Capital of Roman Arabia and the market the Meccan caravans aimed at. Its civic era, epoch 105/106 CE, dates the Namāra, Jabal Usays and Ḥarrān inscriptions.

places.name: al-Jābiya
places.blurb: The Ghassanid royal camp between the Ḥawrān plain and the Golan — a seat of government that was a tent city, not a walled capital. Foreign envoys came out here to meet the kings.

places.name: Jabal Says / Usays
places.blurb: A volcanic hill about 105 km south-east of Damascus, source of the 528 Arabic inscription often called the only pre-Islamic Arabic text with historical content.

places.name: al-Namāra
places.blurb: A basalt site in the Ḥarra about 100 km south-east of Damascus where the funerary stone of Imruʾ al-Qays 'king of all the Arabs' was found. The stone is now in the Louvre.

places.name: Ḥarrān in the Lejā
places.blurb: A village south of Damascus whose martyrium of St John carries a Greek-Arabic bilingual of 568, dated by an Arabian era reckoned from the destruction of Khaybar.

places.name: Yarmūk
places.blurb: The river valley where the Ghassanids and the Byzantine field army were broken in 636, closing the period.

places.name: Petra
places.blurb: The dead Nabataean capital, annexed by Rome in 106, still standing in the landscape as carved facades and high places when travellers of the 6th century rode past.

places.name: Hegra / Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ
places.blurb: 131 rock-cut Nabataean tombs across some 12 km², with Jabal Ithlib as the religious quarter. By the 6th century these were read as the houses of Thamūd, a race annihilated by God — a mistake that was itself a live belief of the period.

places.name: Dadan
places.blurb: The older oasis capital beneath al-ʿUlā, with lion-flanked tombs above it and the god Dhū Ghaybat in its inscriptions. Already a ruin field in late antiquity.

places.name: al-ʿUlā
places.blurb: A long palm oasis on the incense road, with a Jewish population appearing from the 5th century.

places.name: Taymāʾ
places.blurb: A walled oasis on the Syrian road, called a city of the Jews in pre-Islamic verse, with a deep epigraphic past going back to the Babylonians and the god Ṣalm of Maḥram.

places.name: al-Ablaq
places.blurb: Al-Samawʾal's piebald fortress on a hill by Taymāʾ, a staging post for travellers to and from Syria, and the place where he let his son be killed rather than hand over Imruʾ al-Qays's deposits.

places.name: Khaybar
places.blurb: A black-rock oasis of date palms and Jewish settlement. Its 'destruction' around 105 CE was still the epoch of a local dating era in 568.

places.name: Dūmat al-Jandal
places.blurb: The crossroads oasis at the end of Wādī Sirḥān, an annual fair whose sovereignty was contested between the clients of Byzantium and of Persia, with a market known for slaves. The idol Wadd stood here, and a Christian Arabic graffito of 548/9 was found nearby.

places.name: Wādī Sirḥān
places.blurb: The long depression carrying the route from the Gulf and inner Arabia up into southern Syria.

places.name: Ruwāfa
places.blurb: Ruins of a temple dedicated in 165–169 by 'the Thamūd of Robathū' with Roman backing — hard evidence that the people the Qurʾān calls annihilated were serving in Roman auxiliary units.

places.name: Yathrib / Medina
places.blurb: A spread of fortified farmsteads and palm groves held by Aws and Khazraj alongside three Jewish tribes, exhausted by a century of feuding by 617.

places.name: Buʿāth
places.blurb: The field near Medina where Aws beat Khazraj in the last fight before Islam. Its exact position relative to the oasis is not given in the sources.

places.name: Mecca
places.blurb: A sanctuary town in a dry valley, run by Quraysh clans around the Kaʿba and its idols. There is no inscription, no dig and no outside document for Mecca before 632 — everything about it is literary.

places.name: ʿArafāt
places.blurb: The plain outside the Meccan sacred zone where pilgrims stood in adoration — and which the Ḥums of Quraysh refused to leave their ḥaram to visit.

places.name: Minā
places.blurb: The valley where pilgrims sacrificed, and where the tashrīq days were counted out after the tenth of Dhū al-Ḥijja.

places.name: al-Ṭāʾif
places.blurb: A cool, walled fruit-growing town above Mecca, home of Thaqīf and of Allāt's cubic rock, and Mecca's commercial rival on the road from Yemen.

places.name: ʿUkāẓ
places.blurb: The great fair between Nakhla and al-Ṭāʾif, running twenty-one days each year in Dhū al-Qaʿda before the pilgrimage. Trade, treaties, lawsuits, sport, recited poetry — and the ground most of the Fijār blood was spilled on.

places.name: Majanna
places.blurb: A fair held near Mecca in the same season as ʿUkāẓ and competing with it. Its site is not fixed.

places.name: Dhū al-Majāz
places.blurb: The third of the Meccan-season fairs, held close to the pilgrimage stations. Its site is not fixed.

places.name: Nakhla
places.blurb: Valley on the Mecca–Ṭāʾif side where Hawāzin fell on Quraysh and Kināna, who got away into the sanctuary at nightfall.

places.name: Shamṭa
places.blurb: A Fijār field near ʿUkāẓ, won by Hawāzin.

places.name: al-ʿAblāʾ
places.blurb: A Fijār field at ʿUkāẓ itself, won by Hawāzin.

places.name: al-Ḥurayra
places.blurb: Lava-field ground near ʿUkāẓ where the eighth and last Fijār day was fought.

places.name: al-Mushallal at Qudayd
places.blurb: Manāt's coastal sanctuary between Medina and Mecca, where Aws and Khazraj shaved their heads and without which they did not count a pilgrimage finished.

places.name: Nakhlat al-Shāʾmiyya
places.blurb: The valley of Ḥurāḍ on the Mecca–Iraq road, where al-ʿUzzā had three trees, a house called Buss that gave oracles, a sacred ravine and a killing-ground for sacrifice.

places.name: Ruhāṭ
places.blurb: The seat of the idol Suwāʿ, in Hudhayl country near Yanbuʿ, with the Banū Lihyān as its keepers.

places.name: Tabāla
places.blurb: The white quartz block called Dhū al-Khalaṣa, the 'southern Kaʿba', on the road between Mecca and Ṣanʿāʾ. Blood-revenge was decided here by three arrows: the enjoiner, the forbidder, the vigilant.

places.name: Jurash
places.blurb: A southern highland town whose people kept the god Yaghūth, named in poetry and in no inscription at all.

places.name: Najrān
places.blurb: A rich oasis city on the Yemen–Ḥijāz road, Christian by the 6th century, with a martyrium called the Kaʿba of Najrān that drew pilgrims for forty years. In 523 its Christians were massacred.

places.name: Ḥimà
places.blurb: A wells-and-rock-art site about 90 km north of Najrān holding the earliest precisely dated Paleo-Arabic inscriptions — 470 and 513 — several of them Christian, cut with big ornate crosses.

places.name: Maʾrib
places.blurb: The old Sabaean capital in its artificial oasis, multi-storey mud brick above a canal network, with the dam upstream and a church built in it by the 520s.

places.name: The Maʾrib dam
places.blurb: A 14-metre earth-and-stone barrage with spillways and sluices, visibly failing across the 6th century: breaches in 449, 450, 542 and 548, repairs in 450 and 557, then an overtopping around 570 that nobody repaired.

places.name: Awām temple / Maḥram Bilqīs
places.blurb: The largest temple complex in South Arabia, Almaqah's house, with an oval wall 757 m round, an alabaster water conduit, a dream-oracle and some twenty thousand burials beside it. Abandoned in the 4th century.

places.name: Sirwāḥ
places.blurb: An Almaqah sanctuary west of Maʾrib with monumental inscriptions — including a seven-tonne block that fell from its plinth in an earthquake.

places.name: Barāqish / Yathill
places.blurb: A Minaean walled town with a sixteen-column temple linked to ʿAthtar and altars with bulls' heads at either end.

places.name: Ṣanʿāʾ
places.blurb: The highland city that overtook Ẓafār as the seat of power, besieged by the Persians in 570 and the capital of Sasanian Yemen thereafter.

places.name: Ẓafār
places.blurb: The Ḥimyarite royal capital in the southern highlands, from which kings of Sabaʾ and dhū-Raydān ruled before the centre of gravity moved north to Ṣanʿāʾ.

places.name: Nāʿiṭ
places.blurb: A highland site about 50 km north of Ṣanʿāʾ. A fragmentary Abraha inscription published in 2025 came from here, and line 5 may — or may not — read 'elephants'.

places.name: Murayghān
places.blurb: Where Abraha's northern campaign inscriptions were cut, including the one dated 552 that records his fourth raid on Maʿadd and never mentions Mecca.

places.name: Aksum
places.blurb: The Christian Ethiopian capital across the Red Sea, which invaded Yemen in the 520s and whose soldiers then defected to Abraha and stayed.

places.name: Adulis
places.blurb: Aksum's Red Sea port, from which the fleets crossed to Yemen.

places.name: Ḥaḍramawt
places.blurb: The long southern wadi country, the god Sayīn's land, and where the Kinda withdrew when their power in Najd collapsed.

places.name: Qaryat al-Fāw
places.blurb: A caravan city on the edge of the Empty Quarter with five temples, seventeen or more wells, and the only painted human figures from the Arabian interior — banqueters, camel drivers, vine scrolls in white, ochre, red and black. Abandoned around the 5th century when the water ran out.

places.name: Shiʿb Jabala
places.blurb: An isolated mountain pass in Banū ʿĀmir country, said to be about 150 km south of ʿUnayza, where Kindite power in northern Arabia was broken. The site itself is not identified.

places.name: ʿUnayza
places.blurb: A Najd settlement used by the sources as the landmark from which Shiʿb Jabala is measured.

places.name: Najd
places.blurb: The central plateau: gravel plains, red sand, scattered wells, and the tribal country where almost every named fighting day of the Arabs was fought.

places.name: al-Yamāma
places.blurb: South-eastern Najd, Banū Ḥanīfa country — settled farmers with date groves and wheat fields who supplied grain to Mecca, not nomads.

places.name: Hajar
places.blurb: The chief town of al-Yamāma and the seat of its governor. Its position is not securely fixed.

places.name: Falj
places.blurb: A valley of wells in al-Yamāma, where the first fighting of the Basūs war was done at ʿUnayza and where Musaylima later proclaimed himself a prophet.

places.name: Hajar of al-Baḥrayn
places.blurb: The oasis seat of eastern Arabia under Lakhmid and Sasanian authority, with a bishop in the synod records from 410 onward.

places.name: al-Mushaqqar
places.blurb: A fortress in Hajar of al-Baḥrayn where a Persian commander and Khusraw's agent in al-Yamāma drew the Banū Tamīm in on a promise of grain, killed them in small parties, and then shut the gates on the rest. Unlocated.

places.name: al-Baḥrayn
places.blurb: The eastern coastal province — palm oases, pearl banks, a Persian governor and a scatter of Nestorian bishoprics.

places.name: Mashmahig
places.blurb: An island see of the Church of the East in the Gulf, named in the synods from 410.

places.name: Dārayn / Tarout
places.blurb: A Gulf island port and bishopric on the eastern trade run.

places.name: Ṣuḥār
places.blurb: Oman's main port, looking east to India and north to the Gulf.

places.name: Hormuz
places.blurb: The Persian side of the strait, where the Gulf shipping funnelled through.

places.name: Fulayj
places.blurb: A late Sasanian fort on the Omani coast — the hardest archaeological evidence of Persian military presence in Arabia.

places.name: Oman / Mazūn
places.blurb: The Sasanian province of the south-east, with its own Christian diocese of Beth Mazūnāyē.

places.name: Ḥāʾil
places.blurb: The oasis under the twin mountains of Ṭayyiʾ, where ʿAntara is said to have died and where Ḥātim was buried.

places.name: Tuwārin
places.blurb: The burial place of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī near Ḥāʾil, though other traditions put his tomb elsewhere.

places.name: Qusayba
places.blurb: A place in the Qaṣīm given as ʿAntara's birthplace.

places.name: Wādī ʿAbqar
places.blurb: A deep valley in Najd where, poets said, a man who sleeps out may be visited by a jinnī who teaches him verse. Nothing confirms it was ever a real identifiable place.

places.name: The Sarawāt
places.blurb: The western mountain spine, cooler and wetter than the plains, where outlaw bands hid and Azd and Khathʿam ranged.

places.name: Khazāz
places.blurb: A mountain on the road between Baṣra and Mecca, behind the desert of Munʿij, where Maʿadd lit beacons for three nights and refused to be eaten by the people of Yemen.

places.name: al-Kulāb
places.blurb: A water between Kūfa and Baṣra, remembered as 'the stones of al-Kulāb', where two sons of the Kindite king set matching bounties on each other's heads.

places.name: Raḥraḥān
places.blurb: Fighting ground at 'the nearest waters of Banū Dārim' in Najd, where Maʿbad ibn Zurāra was taken and died a prisoner. The sources name no toponym and disagree about who won.

places.name: Dhū Najab
places.blurb: Where the Yarbūʿ of Tamīm took their revenge a year after Shiʿb Jabala.

places.name: al-Habāʾa
places.blurb: A well in Fazāra country, and the dramatic centre of the Dāḥis war: morning-to-noon fighting in summer heat, oaths and curses at the water's edge, and a mutilated body.

places.name: Dhū Ḥusā
places.blurb: The one clear defeat ʿAbs took in the Dāḥis sequence, still being thrown at them in verse a generation later.

places.name: al-Muraqqab
places.blurb: First day of the ordered Dāḥis list, ʿAbs over Fazāra.

places.name: al-Farūq
places.blurb: A day won by ʿAbs over a Kindite leader and the people of Hajar — though another list makes it a Qays-against-Tamīm day entirely.

places.name: al-Raqam
places.blurb: Listed inside the Dāḥis cycle but actually Ghaṭafān over Banū ʿĀmir — a day-name that has drifted.

places.name: ʿArāʿir
places.blurb: A day whose loser the sources cannot agree on: one has the chief of Kalb killed here, another has Fazāra beating ʿAbs.

places.name: al-Nahy
places.blurb: A water where Banū Shaybān were camped, and the Basūs war's first or second great day depending on which source you take.

places.name: al-Dhanāʾib
places.blurb: Called the greatest encounter of the Basūs war. One source instead uses the name for the spot where Jassās speared Kulayb.

places.name: Wāridāt
places.blurb: Slaughter among Bakr, and the day al-Muhalhil stood over Hammām ibn Murra's body and composed an elegy for the man he had killed.

places.name: al-Quṣaybāt
places.blurb: A beating so bad Bakr thought they would never get up from it — though one source reverses the outcome.

places.name: Quḍa
places.blurb: Also called Taḥlāq al-Limam, the shaving of the forelocks: Bakr shaved their heads to know one another, and their women went among the wounded with water and clubs.

places.name: al-Fuṣayl
places.blurb: The last day of the Basūs war, named 'the camel calf' — the same creature whose killing is said to have started it.

places.name: ʿAyn Ubāgh
places.blurb: A spring at Dhāt al-Khiyār, out in the steppe between Syria and Iraq, where the Lakhmid al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ was killed and his army broken.

places.name: al-Sullān
places.blurb: A valley of water and halfa grass in Tihāma beside Mount Khazāz, on Yāqūt's description. There are two days of this name and the sources confuse them constantly; the second was fought in a different valley, one belonging to Banū ʿAmr of Tamīm, and is also called Yawm al-Sūbān and Qāʿ al-Qurayṭayn.

places.name: al-Nisār
places.blurb: A day of Ḍabba and Banū Tamīm, surviving only as an index entry in two medieval lists.

places.name: Ṭikhfa
places.blurb: Where Banū Yarbūʿ beat a Lakhmid king — the sources disagree over whether it was the father or the son.

places.name: Awāra
places.blurb: Two days of the same name, one against Bakr under al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ, the second against Tamīm under his son ʿAmr ibn Hind.

places.name: Ghār Ḥirāʾ on Jabal al-Nūr
places.blurb: A cave near the summit of a steep hill about three kilometres north-east of the Meccan sanctuary. The tradition has Muḥammad withdrawing there for stretches at a time before the revelation began, which is in keeping with the solitary retreat (taḥannuth) the sīra reports of other Meccans as well.

places.name: al-Ḥanw
places.blurb: A day of the Basūs war that Ibn al-Athīr names and the English reconstruction left out altogether. He gives it no location; the point on the map only holds it among the other days of the war. Al-Aʿshā uses the same name — 'the battle of al-Ḥinw' — for Dhū Qār, so the name was re-used.

places.name: al-Naqiyya
places.blurb: Another Basūs day named by Ibn al-Athīr and missing from the English reconstruction. No location is given for it in any source; the point only holds its place in the sequence.

events.title: Rome annexes Nabataea
events.dateNote: Fixed in the Roman record; the Bostran era that dates four of this file's inscriptions counts from it.
events.summary: Trajan absorbed the Nabataean kingdom. Its era, counted from this annexation, is what dates the Namāra, Jabal Usays, Ḥimà and Ḥarrān inscriptions three and four centuries later — and its tombs and high places were still standing in the landscape the whole time.
events.dispute: Outside the window, included because the Bostran era and the Nabataean ruins layer both run right through the period.

events.title: The Thamūd dedicate a temple at Ruwāfa
events.dateNote: Dated by the reigning emperors named in the Greek text, which gives a window in the 160s rather than a year.
events.summary: A bilingual Greek and Nabataean Aramaic inscription records that 'the Thamūd of Robathū' built a temple with Roman support. They were Roman auxiliary troops. The people the Qurʾān and the pre-Islamic poets both treat as annihilated in the deep past were a going concern in the 2nd century — and the ruined-civilisation belief about them was itself live in the 6th.
events.dispute: Outside the dataset's 300–640 window, included because it is the hard counter-evidence to the Thamūd legend that characters in the period believed. 'Thamudic' as an epigraphic label is a misnomer with no demonstrated link to the tribe.

events.title: Zenobia at Mārid Castle
events.dateNote: Placed by Zenobia's floruit; no source dates the siege itself.
events.summary: Zenobia of Palmyra mentioned the oasis city, and the fortress of Mārid is said to have held out against her attack. A standing building with a named siege attached.
events.dispute: Just before the window; the Palmyrene layer is part of what the period inherited.

events.title: Ḥimyar swallows Sabaʾ
events.dateNote: Placed inside Shammar Yuharʿish's conventional reign of 275-300; the Ḥimyar literature declines a precise year.
events.summary: Shammar Yuharʿish finished what his house had begun and brought Sabaʾ, with Qatabān and Ḥaḍramawt already taken, under one crown at Ẓafār. From here the kings style themselves of Sabaʾ and dhū-Raydān.
events.dispute: The ruler list gives Shammar 275–300; the Ḥimyar article says 'around 280' or 'late 3rd century' and declines the precise year.

sources.title: Shammar Yahri'sh
sources.note: First attested 275 CE; first king to bear the title of Sabaʾ, dhū-Raydān, Ḥaḍramawt and Yamnat; had united most of Yemen by c. 280.
sources.noteAr: أولُ ذكرٍ له في النقوش سنة 275م، وهو أول من حمل لقب ملك سبأ وذي ريدان وحضرموت ويمنت، ووحّد معظم اليمن نحو 280م.

events.title: Namāra inscription
events.dateNote: Fixed by the Bostran era date cut on the stone: 7 Kaslūl, year 223.
events.summary: A funerary stone cut on 7 Kaslūl, year 223 of the Bosra era, for Imruʾ al-Qays son of ʿAmr, called king of all the Arabs. It says he broke the Asad, drove Madhḥij to the gates of Najrān, subdued Maʿadd, and set tribal nobles over them who then served Rome as phylarchs. It is the hardest single date in the whole 4th-century Arabian record and it is now in the Louvre.
events.dispute: The reading is J. A. Bellamy's from 1985 and replaced earlier, different readings; part of the royal title still carries a question mark. It also makes a Lakhmid-line king Roman-facing, which cuts against the Arabic tradition's picture of the Lakhmids as Persian clients throughout.

sources.title: Namarah Inscription: The Second Oldest Dated Pre-Islamic Arabic Inscription (328 CE)

events.title: The last pagan inscription at Maʾrib
events.ar: آخر نقش وثني في معبد مأرب
events.dateNote: Era conversion puts the temple's last dated polytheistic text in 379/380.
events.summary: The last dated polytheistic text in Maʾrib's Great Temple. Most South Arabian temples were already deserted. A story set in 6th-century Yemen should not have a functioning Almaqah cult in it — that world had closed two hundred years earlier.

sources.title: Diversity and Rabbinization - 7. The Judaism of the Ancient Kingdom of Ḥimyar in Arabia

events.title: Ḥimyar turns to the Lord of the Sky
events.dateNote: Fixed at the near end by the royal inscriptions of January 384; the window opens with the 379/380 silence, and Robin allows an earlier start.
events.summary: Royal inscriptions of January 384 drop the ancestral gods and invoke 'the Lord of the Sky'. Within a generation the kingdom's public religion is Judaic monotheism — about 140 to 150 inscriptions document it over the next century and a half, and not one of them states a creed.
events.dispute: Robin keeps the 380–384 window but allows an earlier start. Whether this Judaism was rabbinic is a live dispute: Robin reads it as priestly and non-rabbinic because the texts never mention resurrection; Gajda reads it as rabbinic.

sources.title: Diversity and Rabbinization - 7. The Judaism of the Ancient Kingdom of Ḥimyar in Arabia

events.title: Yawm Khazāz
events.dateNote: Undated in every source. Placed early because Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ argued the day was older than any of the men credited with leading it.
events.summary: Maʿadd refused to be eaten by the people of Yemen. A Yemeni collector used to arrive with a scribe and a carpet to sit on and take whatever he liked of Nizār's property. They lit a fire on the mountain for three nights and made smoke for three days, and the tribes came in.
events.dispute: The leadership is a genuine scholarly argument preserved verbatim: a Friday circle at Baṣra disputed whether al-Aḥwaṣ ibn Jaʿfar, Kulayb ibn Wāʾil or Zurāra ibn ʿUdus led there. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ruled against all three on the grounds that the day is older than those men, and said he had been asking for sixty years and had never found anybody who knew its chief. The ʿIqd page also notes the day would not be known at all but for one line of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm's verse — the page is cut off before the battle itself. Undated.

sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.title: ج6 - ص97 - كتاب العقد الفريد - يوم خزاز

events.title: A bishop of al-Ḥīra at the synod
events.summary: Bishop Hosea of al-Ḥīra attended the first synod of the Church of the East. The same synod records bishops out at Mashmahig, Dārayn, Hajar and Haṭṭā — so the Gulf littoral already had a church structure in 410.

events.title: Raḥmānān appears
events.dateNote: A midpoint of the window in which RḤMNN starts appearing in the inscriptions.
events.summary: The divine name RḤMNN enters the Ḥimyarite inscriptions, alternating with Īlān and the plural Aʾlāhān. It is the same name the Qurʾān will use two centuries later as al-Raḥmān.

sources.title: Diversity and Rabbinization - 7. The Judaism of the Ancient Kingdom of Ḥimyar in Arabia

events.title: Yawm al-Sullān I
events.dateNote: Undated; a placement inside the 5th century, and the compilers themselves confuse al-Sullān I with al-Sullān II.
events.summary: Maʿadd against the people of Yemen in a valley of water and halfa grass beside Mount Khazāz, between the Ḥijāz and Yemen. Victory to Maʿadd.
events.dispute: Leadership contested three ways, and Yāqūt makes the opponents Madhḥij and Kalb. The Muʿjam al-Asāṭīr compiler explicitly accuses Jawād ʿAlī of confusing al-Sullān I with al-Sullān II, and al-Maydānī of the same error. Undated.

sources.title: مدونة محمد مفرج السيد الرديني : السلان ( يوم السلان )

events.title: Ḥimyar sets Ḥujr over the Maʿadd
events.dateNote: The Arabic sources date the founding of Kindite kingship to 425 and run Ḥujr's reign 425-458; the English ones say no regnal dates exist for him and infer a window from Abīkarib's conventional reign of c. 390-440. The year here is now the Arabic 425, with the inferred window kept as the range.
events.summary: A Ḥimyarite king campaigned into central Arabia and installed Ḥujr Ākil al-Murār — 'eater of bitter herbs' — over the Maʿadd tribes. Kinda's kingship begins here, as a southern crown's instrument for governing nomads. The Arabic sources name the sponsor as Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr ibn Tubbāʿ and put it in 425.
events.dispute: The English sources state flatly that no regnal dates exist for Ḥujr and infer the window from his Ḥimyarite sponsor's reign, conventionally c. 390–440; they also name that sponsor Abīkarib Asʿad. The Arabic sources give a founding year, 425, a sponsor, Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr ibn Tubbāʿ, and a full regnal series after it — Ḥujr 425–458, ʿAmr 458–489, al-Ḥārith 489–528. Nothing external confirms any of it. He is said to have reigned long and died of old age at Baṭn ʿAqīl, which does not sit easily with a reign ending in a fixed year.

events.title: The dam breaks
events.dateNote: Fixed by the dam inscriptions, which record breaches in two consecutive years.
events.summary: Two major breaches in consecutive years tore the Maʾrib barrage open. The first failure of the century, and the first one the kingdom was still strong enough to answer.

events.title: Yawm al-Bardān
events.dateNote: Undated; known only from a one-line entry in al-Khāqānī's list, so the year is a placement.
events.summary: Ḥujr Ākil al-Murār of Kinda over Zayd ibn al-Habūla of Quḍāʿa — a purely southern-Arabian day with no northern party in it at all.
events.dispute: Known only from al-Khāqānī's one-line entry. Undated.

events.title: Sharaḥbiʾīl Yaʿfar rebuilds the dam
events.dateNote: Fixed by the repair inscription.
events.summary: The king put the barrage back up. Six hundred years of this cycle lie behind the repair and only a century of it lies ahead.

events.title: Qaryat al-Fāw runs dry
events.dateNote: Dated only as 'around the 5th century'; 450 is the midpoint of that century.
events.summary: A caravan city that had stood for nearly a thousand years — five temples, a market, seventeen or more wells, painted banqueters on its walls — was abandoned when its water was irreversibly depleted. For a story opening around 400–500 this is a great city dying inside living memory.
events.dispute: Dated only as 'around the 5th century'. The same site article has the Kinda leaving around 300, which makes the common claim that Fāw was the capital of a 450–550 Kindite kingdom almost certainly a conflation of two phases a century and a half apart.

sources.title: Cultural Landscape of Al-Faw Archaeological Area — UNESCO World Heritage List

events.title: CIH 540 cut on the dam
events.dateNote: Fixed by the inscription's own Ḥimyarite era date.
events.summary: A dated Judaic royal inscription on the Maʾrib dam, one of the clearest markers that the kings who maintained the waterworks were by now monotheists.

sources.title: Diversity and Rabbinization - 7. The Judaism of the Ancient Kingdom of Ḥimyar in Arabia

events.title: ẒM 1
events.dateNote: Fixed by the inscription's own Ḥimyarite era date.
events.summary: Another dated Judaic royal Ḥimyarite text, part of the thin but real spine of hard dates that South Arabia gives and the rest of the peninsula does not.

sources.title: Diversity and Rabbinization - 7. The Judaism of the Ancient Kingdom of Ḥimyar in Arabia

events.title: Ḥimà-Sud PalAr 1
events.dateNote: Fixed by the era date in the inscription itself.
events.summary: The earliest precisely dated Paleo-Arabic inscription, cut at Ḥimà about 90 km north of Najrān, Christian, with big ornate crosses. A literate, Arabic-writing Christian Arabian, a century before Muḥammad, with a date on him.

events.title: ʿAmr al-Maqṣūr killed by the Rabīʿa
events.dateNote: The Arabic sources end his reign in 489, which is the year used here; the English ones have only 'probably killed in battle against the Rabīʿa in the late 5th century'.
events.summary: Ḥujr's successor in Najd was rejected by the Rabīʿa tribes and probably killed fighting them. Kindite authority over the north was never again uncontested.
events.dispute: No external attestation. The Arabic regnal series — Ḥujr 425–458, ʿAmr 458–489, al-Ḥārith 489–528 — is the only thing that dates this, and the English sources say outright that they found no dates for these kings. The Arabic sources also write the epithet al-Manṣūr rather than al-Maqṣūr.

events.title: Kulayb kills the she-camel, Jassās kills Kulayb
events.dateNote: The killing itself is undated; the only date anywhere in the corpus is the war's overall 494-534 span, from one modern Arabic compilation, and endYear carries that span so the war can be drawn as a band.
events.summary: Kulayb ibn Rabīʿa, lord of Taghlib, enforced his reserved pasture with a stake and a puppy and was hated for it. He shot a she-camel that had strayed among Jassās ibn Murra's herd under the protection of al-Basūs. Her lament went round the camps, Jassās speared Kulayb, Jassās's father refused to hand his son over, and forty years of war followed.
events.dispute: The camel is itself two stories welded together: Ibn al-Athīr makes her Sarāb, property of Saʿd ibn Shumays al-Jarmī, sheltered by al-Basūs who was Jassās's maternal aunt; al-Maʿrifa gives her no name, makes her al-Basūs's own, and has Kulayb shoot her calf first and then her udder. Modern scholarship treats the whole war as a composite of separate raid-stories, not one conflict.

events.title: Yawm ʿUnayza
events.dateNote: Undated. The year holds the day's place in the sequence the sources do give, which is worth more than any year.
events.summary: The first fighting of the Basūs war, at Falj in al-Yamāma. The two sides were evenly matched and parted without a winner.
events.dispute: Ibn al-Athīr calls it the first engagement; al-Maʿrifa gives that place to al-Nahy instead. Undated.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Yawm al-Nisār
events.dateNote: No source gives a date, a place or a narrative; 500 is a bare midpoint of the period.
events.summary: A day of Ḍabba and Banū Tamīm.
events.dispute: Listed in the contents of both Ibn al-Athīr and al-ʿIqd al-Farīd and in al-Qalqashandī's roll, with no narrative recovered anywhere and no date. The year here is a bare midpoint of the period, not an estimate.

events.title: Yawm al-Nahy
events.dateNote: Undated, and al-Maʿrifa makes this the war's first engagement rather than its second; the year only holds a place in the sequence.
events.summary: At a water called al-Nahy where Banū Shaybān were camped. Al-Muhalhil led Taghlib against al-Ḥārith ibn Murra. Hard fighting, and not one man of Banū Murra was killed that day. Taghlib took it.
events.dispute: Undated. Al-Maʿrifa makes this the war's first engagement rather than its second.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Qusayy takes the Kaʿba
events.dateNote: Meccan chronology before c. 600 is unanchored: Hawting's reading puts Qusayy's children in the later 5th century, Watt's puts Qusayy's own death in the later 6th.
events.summary: Qusayy ibn Kilāb pulled the scattered descendants of Fihr together and took control of the sanctuary, and the order of Meccan clan offices descends from him.
events.dispute: The internal contradiction here is a full century wide. Hawting says that if the traditional sources are believed Qusayy's children must have lived in the second half of the fifth century; Watt says Qusayy himself likely died in the second half of the sixth. Nothing resolves it, so Meccan internal chronology before about 600 is effectively free, provided the sequence Qusayy to ʿAbd Manāf to Hāshim to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stays intact.

events.title: Kinda become Byzantine federates
events.summary: Byzantium took the Kinda into treaty as federates. For a while al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr held a Ḥimyarite mandate, a Byzantine treaty and a phylarchate in Palestine at the same time — which is probably why Kinda fractured faster than any other buffer power.

events.title: Al-Mundhir III raids the Roman frontier
events.summary: The Lakhmid king struck into Palaestina Salutaris and Arabia Petraea during the Anastasian War. From 503 onward the external sources constrain Lakhmid history year by year; before him it is free narrative space.

events.title: Yawm al-Dhanāʾib
events.dateNote: Undated; the year holds the day's place in the sequence, nothing more.
events.summary: Called the greatest encounter of the whole war. Many of Bakr were killed, including al-Ḥārith ibn Murra and ʿAmr ibn Sadūs. Taghlib's high point.
events.dispute: Undated. Al-Maʿrifa uses the same place-name for the spot where Jassās speared Kulayb, which is a different use entirely.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Yawm Wāridāt
events.dateNote: Undated, and the sources cannot agree where Hammām died; the year holds the day's place in the sequence.
events.summary: Heavy slaughter among Bakr. Hammām ibn Murra was killed — by Nāshira, a Taghlibī he had raised himself — and al-Muhalhil stood over the body and composed an elegy for his own enemy.
events.dispute: Undated, and the sources cannot agree where Hammām died: Wāridāt, al-Quṣaybāt or Quḍa. Al-Maʿrifa puts a single combat between Jassās and Abū Nuwayra on this day instead.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Zabad inscription
events.dateNote: Fixed by the inscription's own date.
events.summary: A trilingual lintel on the martyrium of St Sergius, Greek and Syriac and Paleo-Arabic, dated year 823 of the Seleucid era. The Greek names the clergy, donors and the architects Symeon and Leontius; the Arabic simply asks God to remember a list of men. It is the earliest dated Paleo-Arabic text, and it opens by seeking help from al-ilāh.

events.title: The second Ḥimà group
events.dateNote: Fixed by the era dates in the inscriptions.
events.summary: A further set of Paleo-Arabic inscriptions at Ḥimà, dated by the Bostran era. One of them calls its writer 'servant of Christ'.

events.title: Yawm al-Quṣaybāt
events.dateNote: Undated, and the two main sources reverse the outcome; the year holds the day's place in the sequence.
events.summary: Bakr were hit so hard they thought they would never recover.
events.dispute: Undated. Ibn al-Athīr gives the day to Taghlib; al-Maʿrifa reverses the outcome and also states flatly that Hammām was killed here, where Ibn al-Athīr says only 'it is also said'.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Dhū Nuwās takes the Ḥimyarite throne
events.dateNote: 519 is a midpoint. The reported accession dates are 517, 522 and '518 or 522', and 519 is none of them.
events.summary: Yūsuf Asʾar Yathʾar, called Dhū Nuwās, seized power as the last native Ḥimyarite king, displacing an Aksumite client. His reign runs straight into the Najrān killings and the Ethiopian invasion.
events.dispute: Three incompatible accession dates circulate across two reference articles: 517, 522, and '518 or 522'. Munro-Hay's 525 date for the Aksumite conquest depends on an 518 accession; a 523 accession pushes the conquest to about 530. The end of the reign is contested the same way: the Arabic sources give 517–527 with the death 'at the Red Sea' in 527, against 530 in the English ones, and one Arabic article has him born in 468 in its lead and in 450 in its sidebar.

events.title: Jabalah IV's camp at al-Jābiya
events.dateNote: Placed by Simeon of Bēth Arshām's letter, which is itself dated only to about 518-522.
events.summary: A letter of Simeon of Bēth Arshām places the Ghassanid king's camp at al-Jābiya. Not a palace and not a walled capital — a royal tent city between the Ḥawrān and the Golan, which is what the Ghassanid state actually was.

events.title: Ḥimyar wipes out Jadīs
events.dateNote: Undated, and the akhbār place these peoples both in the deep past and inside living memory of the 6th century.
events.summary: The tyrant of Ṭasm claimed the right to the brides of Jadīs before their husbands. At a performance the men of Jadīs drew swords they had buried in the sand and killed him. Ḥimyar came in reprisal: a woman of Jadīs warned her people of the invasion and was ignored, the adults were slaughtered and the children taken.
events.dispute: The akhbār's chronology is incoherent on purpose: Ṭasm and Jadīs are called contemporaries of ʿĀd and Thamūd, in the deep past, yet destroyed in the 6th century within living memory of the period. Al-Ṭabarī's version makes the reprisal payback for the killing of a Ḥimyarite ally. The tyrant is named ʿImlīq; the 'tyrant of Jaww' framing could not be verified.

events.title: Zarqāʾ al-Yamāma is not believed
events.dateNote: Undated; placed with the destruction of Jadīs, a join the sources do not actually make.
events.summary: The blue-eyed woman of al-Yamāma could see riders a week away. The enemy advanced hidden behind trees they carried, and she warned that the trees were moving, and her people thought she was going mad. After the camp's men were killed the invaders tore out her eyes and crucified her.
events.dispute: Her story's sourcing is weak — a comparative-literature book and a newspaper feature, neither a specialist source — and the sight-range is given as a week, not the three days often repeated. The Ṭasm and Jadīs page does not mention her at all while her page makes her a Jadīsī, so the traditional join between the two stories could not be verified.

events.title: Ḥimyar drives the Lakhmids out of Najd
events.summary: Central Arabian tribes appealed south, and Ḥimyar pushed Lakhmid power back out of the plateau. The interior was a theatre both client systems fought over, not an empty middle.

events.title: The Najrān massacre
events.dateNote: The killings are dated 523; the destruction of the town is separately dated to Tuesday, 15 Tishrī, Seleucid 835, which is 524.
events.summary: Dhū Nuwās put down a revolt at Najrān and had al-Ḥārith and some three hundred and forty of his followers killed, in November by one reckoning. Three Sabaic inscriptions bear on it, one of them dated June or July of that year — and they are political texts that barely mention religion at all.
events.dispute: The killings are dated 523 and the destruction of the town separately to a Tuesday, 15 Tishrī, Seleucid 835, which is 524. The death toll is the clearest case of inflation in the whole record, and it inflates in three stages, not two: about 200 in the sources written soon after the event, eleven thousand in the Arabic sources — which say Dhū Nuwās's force at Najrān pulled down the bishopric, killed its bishop and eleven thousand Christians, and put the total killed across his campaigns against the Christians of Yemen at twenty-two thousand — and seventy thousand in sources written centuries later. The Arabic sources warn in the same breath that the Syriac accounts may have exaggerated. Robin warns that the Christian accounts frame a political repression as a religious war. The three Christian witnesses are Simeon of Bēth Arshām's letter of January 524, the Syriac Book of the Ḥimyarites, and the Martyrdom of Arethas; of the two published letters, only one may carry historical value and the attribution of the others is contested.

events.title: Simeon of Bēth Arshām writes from al-Ḥīra
events.summary: In January, in the Lakhmid capital, a Miaphysite bishop wrote down what had happened at Najrān within months of its happening. It is the nearest thing to a contemporary document that pre-Islamic Arabia produced, and it was written at the court of the Persians' Arab king.
events.dispute: Two further letters were published separately, by Guidi in 1881 and Shahîd in 1971. Only the original 'Letter C' may have historical value; the authorship of the others is disputed.

events.title: Aksum invades Yemen
events.dateNote: A real 525-543 spread in the scholarship, turning on which accession date is taken for Dhū Nuwās. 525 is Procopius's.
events.summary: King Kāleb sent an army across the Red Sea at Justin I's request. Dhū Nuwās was killed, the native Ḥimyarite kingship ended, and Ethiopian Christian rule began in South Arabia.
events.dispute: A real 525–543 spread. Munro-Hay dates it 525 on an 518 accession for Dhū Nuwās; a 523 accession gives about 530; Jacques Ryckmans has suggested as late as 543. Procopius is the source for 525. The Arabic sources put Dhū Nuwās's death in 527 rather than 530, which is a fourth figure inside the same argument.

events.title: Yawm Quḍa, the shaving of the forelocks
events.dateNote: Undated; the year holds the day's place in the sequence. The sources disagree even on whose son Bujayr was.
events.summary: Bakr shaved their heads so they would know each other in the press — in readiness for death, one source says — and their women went among the fighters with water and clubs. Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿUbād, who had sat out the whole war, came back to lead them after al-Muhalhil killed the young man he sent with a peace letter. He cut Taghlib to pieces, took al-Muhalhil prisoner, and let him go without recognising him.
events.dispute: Undated. The sources disagree on whether Bujayr was al-Ḥārith's son or his nephew, and on whether he carried a peace offer or an announcement of withdrawal. His killing is the structural hinge of the whole war in both versions: Taghlib wins every day up to it and loses after it.

sources.title: ذكر مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب
sources.author: Ibn al-Athīr, ed. ʿUmar ʿAbd al-Salām Tadmurī
sources.note: Yawm Quḍḍa, also called Taḥlāq al-Limam, where Bakr shaved their heads.
sources.noteAr: يومُ قِضّة، وهو يوم تحلاق اللِّمَم، حين حلقت بكرٌ رؤوسها.

events.title: The Banū Asad kill Ḥujr
events.dateNote: Dated purely by inference from the fall of Kinda's Ḥimyarite sponsor in 525, and it collides with one of the two birth schemes for his son.
events.summary: Ḥujr ibn al-Ḥārith, the Kindite set over the Asad and Ghaṭafān, was killed in an Asad revolt. His son Imruʾ al-Qays was the only one who went after the killers, and the whole vengeance quest that defines Arabic poetry's founding figure starts here.
events.dispute: Dated purely by inference: Kinda's Ḥimyarite sponsor fell to Aksum in 525, so the revolt is placed alongside it. The date collides head-on with one of the two birth schemes for Imruʾ al-Qays, which would make him an infant in 525.

events.title: Al-Shanfarā dies one short
events.dateNote: No dates exist for al-Shanfarā at all; c. 525 is a handbook convention.
events.summary: He had sworn to kill a hundred men of the Azd and died having killed ninety-nine. Later an Azdī man kicked his skull, took a splinter in his foot and died of the infection — which the tradition treats as completing the vow. The unfinished claim of the dead acting in the world, which is the same idea as the thirsty soul-bird of an unavenged killing.
events.dispute: No dates whatsoever exist for al-Shanfarā in the accessible sources; c. 525 is a handbook convention. His tribe, conventionally Azd or Banū Salāmān, is likewise unsourced. The Lāmiyyat al-ʿArab that made him famous has been disputed since medieval times — al-Tibrīzī credited Khalaf al-Aḥmar, a known 8th-century forger of ancient verse.

events.title: Death of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr the Kindite
events.dateNote: Placed c. 528 from the Byzantine notices, which do not fix the year.
events.summary: The best-known Kindite king, and the first attested in Byzantine sources, was killed in the Syrian Desert. His four sons split the Maʿadd command between them and spent the next years killing each other.
events.dispute: The sources cannot agree whether the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III killed him or the Banū Kalb did.

events.title: Jabal Usays inscription
events.dateNote: Fixed by the Bostran era date on the stone.
events.summary: Cut '423 after Bosra' on a volcanic hill about 105 km south-east of Damascus, and described as the only pre-Islamic Arabic inscription with real historical content.
events.dispute: The accessible publication gives the date and findspot but not the text, so the names usually attached to it could not be confirmed.

sources.title: Jabal Usays Inscription: A Pre-Islamic Arabic Inscription From 528 CE

events.title: Battle of Thannuris
events.summary: Belisarius was beaten in upper Mesopotamia and the Ghassanid king Jabalah IV died on the field. His son al-Ḥārith took over the phylarchate.

events.title: Justinian makes al-Ḥārith a king
events.dateNote: His elevation is given as c. 528 in one article and 529 in another; endYear carries his reign to his externally dated death in 569.
events.summary: Justinian raised al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala to kingship and to patrikios, with command over all Byzantium's Arab allies in the East — the highest imperial title ever given a foreign ruler. One Arab king now answered for the whole frontier.
events.dispute: His reign start is given as c. 528 in one article and 529 in another.

events.title: Al-Mundhir III burns through Syria
events.dateNote: The campaign runs across 528-529 in the Greek sources.
events.summary: The Lakhmid took Khabour, raided Arzona and Nisibis, reached Apamea and failed at Antioch, and came home with plunder said to include four hundred nuns, reportedly sacrificed to al-ʿUzzā.
events.dispute: The nun-sacrifice detail comes through hostile Christian reporting and should be handled as what the enemy said about him.

events.title: Yawm al-Fuṣayl
events.dateNote: Undated, and Ibn al-Athīr does no more than name it; the year holds the day's place in the sequence.
events.summary: The last day of the war, won by Bakr. Its name means 'the camel calf' — the same creature one version of the trigger-story has Kulayb shooting first.
events.dispute: Undated, and Ibn al-Athīr does no more than name it. Al-Maʿrifa gives no account of al-Fuṣayl as a day or a place at all. The echo between the name and the trigger-story may be a beautiful irony or may be evidence that the trigger grew backward out of the day-name — that link is inference, not a sourced claim.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Yawm al-Kulāb I
events.dateNote: Entirely undated; the window is a guess at the generation.
events.summary: After the Kindite king died his sons fell out, and Shuraḥbīl marched on his brother Salama with the outcasts who attached themselves to kings. Each side's herald offered a hundred camels for the other brother's head. Taghlib and Salama won the day; a man who had been owed blood-money speared Shuraḥbīl and sent his head to his brother, and Salama wept over it.
events.dispute: Entirely undated. Al-Khāqānī's list locates al-Kulāb as a water between Kūfa and Baṣra and agrees on the outcome; Fajernet gives a different alignment of the tribes.

events.title: Battle of Callinicum
events.summary: Belisarius was defeated on the Euphrates by Persians and Lakhmids and dismissed after an inquiry. Al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala brought five thousand Arabs to the Roman side.
events.dispute: Procopius says the Arabs fled and cost Byzantium the battle; Malalas says al-Ḥārith stood firm while the other Arabs ran. Two contemporary Greek sources in direct contradiction — and al-Ḥārith kept his command either way.

events.title: The Perpetual Peace
events.summary: Khusraw I had just taken the Persian throne and both empires wanted out. Conquests went back, and Byzantium paid eleven thousand pounds of gold. It held for eight years.

events.title: Hujras kills his uncle
events.dateNote: Undated akhbār; placed after the war's main days because that is where the narrative puts it.
events.summary: Jassās had raised Kulayb's son Hujras as his own. When the boy learned who had killed his father he killed Jassās.
events.dispute: Undated akhbār.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Imruʾ al-Qays's war of vengeance
events.dateNote: No dates at all. The episode is akhbār built around the poems, and the late birth scheme for the poet makes it impossible.
events.summary: Asad offered him a choice: kill a noble of his father's rank, take blood-money in sheep and camels, or war. He took war. Bakr and Taghlib rode with him, and then walked away once they judged the revenge sufficient, leaving him with nothing. A Ḥimyarite king is said to have sent him five hundred men.
events.dispute: No dates at all. The whole episode is akhbār built around the poems. It is also the part of his life that the late birth-date of c. 526 makes impossible.

events.title: Al-Muhalhil dies of thirst
events.dateNote: Undated, and the death is told twice with different names; the year only keeps him after the war.
events.summary: After forty years he called his own people to peace and left for Yemen, settled among Janb of Madhḥij and married there. He was taken prisoner near Hajar by a man who had sworn not to give him water until something lost was returned, was handed brackish water, and died of thirst.
events.dispute: Al-Maʿrifa tells the same death with different names — an oath, withheld water, and the thing returned three days too late. Two variants of one story; a dramatist should not name a single canonical captor. Undated.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: The dam breaks again
events.dateNote: Fixed by the dam inscriptions.
events.summary: Ninety years after the last repair the barrage failed again, and this time in the middle of a change of regime.

events.title: Al-Ḥārith asks Theodora for bishops
events.summary: A Miaphysite Arab king petitioned the empress for Miaphysite bishops in Syria, and she appointed Jacob Baradaeus. Jacob went on to build what became the Syriac Orthodox church. It is the most consequential thing any Ghassanid ever did.

events.title: The fair at ʿUkāẓ
events.dateNote: The same article gives 501 as the founding and c. 542-726 as the active period; 542 is the later of the two figures.
events.summary: Twenty-one days every year in Dhū al-Qaʿda, just before the pilgrimage: trade, lawsuits settled, treaties concluded, athletics, recited poetry, preaching. Its position on the western spice route drove its growth through the 6th century.
events.dispute: Founding given as 501 in an infobox and an active period of c. 542–726 in the text of the same article. The familiar claim that poets competed here and the winning ode was hung in the Kaʿba could not be sourced either way, and most scholars reject the Kaʿba part.

events.title: Abraha repairs the dam
events.dateNote: 543 in one source against CIH 541's 548 - either two campaigns of work or one wrong figure.
events.summary: The Ethiopian general turned king of Yemen put the dam back together and celebrated its completion with a mass. The inscription recording it was first published by Eduard Glaser in 1897.
events.dispute: The 543 date clashes with CIH 541's record of repairs in 548. Either two separate campaigns of work, or one of the two dates is wrong; the sources do not resolve it.

events.title: Yawm Awāra I
events.dateNote: Undated; the window is simply al-Mundhir III's reign.
events.summary: Al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ against Banū Bakr.
events.dispute: Undated; the window is simply al-Mundhir III's reign. One of many day-names doubled into a first and second.

sources.title: يوم أوارة الأول
sources.author: Ibn al-Athīr, ed. ʿUmar ʿAbd al-Salām Tadmurī

events.title: CIH 541
events.dateNote: Fixed by the inscription's own Ḥimyarite era date.
events.summary: The dam's key document and the last archaeological reference to it before the end. It lists what the work crews ate — 50,806 measures of flour, 26,000 of dates, meat worth 3,000 cattle, 7,200 small stock, 300 camel-loads of wine — records a plague and Abraha's campaigns, describes a conference of envoys from Aksum, Byzantium, Persia and the Ghassanids, and notes the appointment of a deputy-governor for Kinda.
events.dispute: Abraha's name on line 4 is damaged or erased, possibly deliberately by people who wanted Ethiopian rule forgotten. None of the sub-events in the text carries its own date, and the dam repair is dated 543 in one place and 548 by this inscription — either two work seasons or an error, and the matter is unresolved. A gap in the Arabic reference literature belongs on this record: the general Arabic works never name CIH 541, and never mention the Murayghān inscriptions or the year 552 either. They describe this text accurately without naming it — a tablet at the dam of a hundred and thirty-six lines and about four hundred and seventy words — so the object is known in Arabic and its siglum is not, which is why the epigraphic argument about the Year of the Elephant cannot be followed from Arabic sources alone.

events.title: Breach and rebuilding
events.dateNote: Fixed by CIH 541.
events.summary: Another major breach, answered by the largest documented repair effort of the century.

events.title: Dūmat al-Jandal Christian graffito
events.dateNote: The graffito's own era date, year 443, converts to 548/549.
events.summary: A Paleo-Arabic Christian graffito dated year 443 of its era, published in 2017, opening 'May be remembered. May God remember' a man and his son. Christian Arabic writing in the middle of the northern desert.

events.title: Ry 506 / Murayghān 1
events.dateNote: Fixed by the internal date: year 662 of the Ḥimyarite era, month dhu-ʿallān.
events.summary: Dated internally to year 662, month dhu-ʿallān, which is September 552. Abraha's fourth raid on Maʿadd after the Banū ʿĀmir revolted: Maʿadd beaten, hostages taken, and ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir of al-Ḥīra submitting and handing over his own son. Mecca is not named anywhere in it.
events.dispute: This is the central document of the Year of the Elephant argument — Iwona Gajda accepts 552 as the date of the northern expedition precisely because this is the only dated one. It also puts ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir in the field two years before the conventional table has him taking the Lakhmid throne.

events.title: ʿAmr ibn Hind takes al-Ḥīra
events.dateNote: The conventional table gives 554, but Ry 506 has ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir already acting in 552 - he may have been deputising for his father; endYear carries the reign to his killing, itself given as 568/9, 569 or 570.
events.summary: A man with a violent temper and a Kindite mother came to the Lakhmid throne. His court drew Ṭarafa, al-Mutalammis, al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza and ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm — and he killed one of them and was killed by another.
events.dispute: Ry 506 has him already acting as 'ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir' in 552, before the conventional accession; he may have been deputising for his father.

events.title: Yawm Ḥalīma
events.dateNote: Fixed to June 554 through the Greek account of the battle near Chalcis; identifying that battle with Yawm Ḥalīma is itself a modern reconstruction.
events.summary: In June the Ghassanids broke a Lakhmid army near Chalcis. Al-Mundhir III fell on the field after fifty years of raiding; al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala lost his eldest son Jabala. The day is named for Ḥalīma, al-Ḥārith's own daughter, and it is the one fighting day of the Arabs that can be nailed to an externally dated battle.
events.dispute: The battle near Chalcis in June 554 is externally sourced; the name Yawm Ḥalīma is from the Arabic tradition, so the identification of the two is itself a scholarly reconstruction. One reference article's infobox spreads the battle across Iraq, Jordan and Syria while its text puts it near Chalcis. The Arabic sources identify Ḥalīma as al-Ḥārith's own daughter, which is sharper than the English 'a Ghassanid princess who helped her tribe's fighters'. They also keep Yawm Ḥalīma and Yawm ʿAyn Ubāgh firmly apart, as two consecutive and separate entries: ʿAyn Ubāgh is the killing of al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ, the father, and Marj Ḥalīma the killing of al-Mundhir ibn al-Mundhir, the son — two battles, two generations, the same family and the same Ghassanid enemy.

events.title: Yawm ʿAyn Ubāgh
events.dateNote: Undated in every source reached. Placed between the two Lakhmid generations, since Ibn al-Athīr files it one generation before Marj Ḥalīma.
events.summary: Al-Mundhir camped at the spring and demanded ransom or war. Al-Ḥārith the Ghassanid proposed instead that each side send out a son to single combat, and when the sons were used up the two old men would come out themselves. Al-Mundhir sent a champion dressed as his son; a defector told al-Ḥārith; the armies clashed next day, al-Mundhir was killed, and al-Ḥārith loaded his two dead sons on a camel with the enemy king's corpse on top — the origin of a proverb about the top-load above the two panniers. He then burned al-Ḥīra and buried his sons there.
events.dispute: Undated in every source reached. It is routinely confused with Yawm Ḥalīma in modern writing, but Ibn al-Athīr files them as two consecutive separate chapters, one generation apart: ʿAyn Ubāgh is the killing of al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ, Marj Ḥalīma the killing of his son. The confusion belongs to the secondary literature, not the Arabic sources.

events.title: The last repairs
events.dateNote: Dated by the repair inscription; one brief gives 558 and the publication reads 557.
events.summary: The final recorded work on the Maʾrib dam. After this nobody with the authority to call out the labour is left.

events.title: The record goes dark
events.dateNote: Era conversion gives 559/560.
events.summary: A church inscription is the last known dated Ḥimyarite text. The South Arabian epigraphic record, the only real chronology in Arabia, goes silent ten years before the traditional Year of the Elephant.

events.title: Bāriqī-Robin-Nāʿiṭ 1
events.dateNote: The inscription carries no date; the range is the plausible span of Abraha's northern campaigns.
events.summary: A fragmentary nine-line Sabaic relief from Nāʿiṭ, published in 2025, naming Abraha and describing military activity around Ṣanʿāʾ. Line 5 may read 'elephants' and line 6 'lions'; line 7 has 'Raḥmānān who is in Heaven', a formula previously found mainly in Jewish texts.
events.dispute: The elephant reading is unconfirmed — the word is damaged and its etymology uncertain. If it holds it would be the first epigraphic elephant in South Arabia. Treat as live scholarship. The event's own date is unknown; the range here is the plausible span of Abraha's northern campaigns.

sources.title: Abraha
sources.note: Mentions a newly discovered Ḥimyarite inscription of Abraha that may name elephants. The dedicated article cited before (Bāriqī-Robin-Nāʿiṭ 1) was deleted from Wikipedia on 2026-03-21.
sources.noteAr: يذكر نقشًا حِمْيَريًّا مكتشفًا حديثًا لأبرهة قد يَرِد فيه ذكر الفِيَلة. وقد حُذفت المقالة المخصَّصة التي كانت مَصدرَه (Bāriqī-Robin-Nāʿiṭ 1) من ويكيبيديا في 21 مارس 2026.

sources.title: Fragment of a Ḥimyarite inscription commissioned by King Abraha, with the hypothetical mention of elephants
sources.author: Zāhir ʿĀṭif al-Bāriqī and Christian J. Robin
sources.note: The editio princeps. Cited from a bibliography; the article itself was not consulted for this entry.
sources.noteAr: النشرة الأولى للنقش. نُقل وصفها من ثَبَت مراجع، ولم يُطَّلع على المقالة نفسها لهذا المدخل.

events.title: The war between al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj and Taghlib
events.ar: الحرب بين الحارث الأعرج وبني تغلب
events.dateNote: Undated; the window is al-Ḥārith al-Aʿraj's reign.
events.summary: A separate Ghassanid campaign against Taghlib, in which ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm clashed with al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Shamir.
events.dispute: Known as a chapter heading in Ibn al-Athīr with the names attached; undated. It is the one attested link between ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm and the Ghassanid court.

sources.title: إسلام ويب  - الكامل في التاريخ - ذكر أيام العرب في الجاهلية - ذكر الحرب بين الحارث الأعرج وبني تغلب- الجزء رقم1

events.title: Death of al-Samawʾal at Taymāʾ
events.dateNote: c. 560 is a reconstruction, and it is not known whether Imruʾ al-Qays was alive when the siege happened.
events.summary: The Jewish lord of al-Ablaq died at Taymāʾ, remembered for one refusal: he would not hand over Imruʾ al-Qays's deposits, and watched his besiegers kill his son in front of him rather than break trust. 'More faithful than al-Samawʾal' was still a proverb centuries later.
events.dispute: The c. 560 date is a reconstruction. His genealogy is disputed — Ibn Durayd makes him the son of a priest, al-Jawālīqī gives him a Ghassanid mother and an Azdī father. And it is not known whether Imruʾ al-Qays was alive or dead when the siege happened.

events.title: Yawm Awāra II
events.dateNote: Undated; the window is ʿAmr ibn Hind's reign.
events.summary: ʿAmr ibn Hind against Banū Tamīm.
events.dispute: Undated; the window is ʿAmr ibn Hind's reign.

sources.title: شبكة فجر الثقافية  :: أيام العرب وحروبها

events.title: The Fifty-Year Peace
events.summary: The long war of 540–562 was closed by treaty. It lasted less than a decade.

events.title: Imruʾ al-Qays reaches Constantinople
events.dateNote: Dated only backward from the poet's death, which is itself given across 561-565 - and the Arabic dating of his life to 496-544 removes the embassy from the record altogether.
events.summary: Carrying a letter of introduction through Ghassanid territory, the dispossessed Kindite prince reached Justinian and came away with promises and perhaps some troops. Justinian is said to have asked Aksum to back him, and Aksum refused because of its feud with Kinda.
events.dispute: The journey is akhbār, not record, and one of the three date-schemes abolishes it. The Arabic sources put the poet's life at 496–544, which would have him dead seventeen years before the embassy; on the early English birth scheme he is a man of sixty-three or sixty-four making a diplomatic trip across the world; on the late one he is the right age but was an infant when his father was killed. The mediator is named in the Arabic sources as al-Ḥārith, the Ghassanid king.

events.title: Imruʾ al-Qays dies near Ankara
events.dateNote: Given across 561-565; no source fixes the year. The Arabic sources date his death to 544 instead, which is a third chronology rather than a variant of this one.
events.summary: He fell ill on the road home and died in Anatolia. The story says Justinian sent him a poisoned robe over an affair at court; most historians think it was the chronic skin disease he names in his own verse. A statue was later said to stand at his tomb, still visible in 1262.
events.dispute: The poisoned robe is an international folklore type, the 'poison dress', not a story specific to him; use it as in-world rumour, which is exactly what it was. The Arabic sources give 544 for the death, not 565 — a figure that cancels the embassy to Constantinople entirely and is the sharpest conflict to come out of the Arabic review. The skin disease is the usual explanation and gives him the epithet Dhū al-Qurūḥ, the man of ulcers. It is also not known whether he died before or after the siege of al-Ablaq in which al-Samawʾal's son was killed over his pledges.

events.title: ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm kills the king at dinner
events.dateNote: Given as 568/9 in one source and 569 or 570 in another.
events.summary: Hind insulted the poet's mother. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm of Taghlib killed the Lakhmid king at his own table for it, and rode out of al-Ḥīra. His brother Qābūs took the throne.
events.dispute: Given as 568/9 in one source and 569 or 570 in another.

events.title: The rigged horse race
events.dateNote: The race is undated; the war's conventional bracket of c. 568-609 is Sir William Muir's Victorian reconstruction rather than a source date, and endYear carries that bracket so the war can be drawn as a band.
events.summary: Before the horses there was a coat of mail. Qays ibn Zuhayr of ʿAbs bought one from Uḥayḥa ibn al-Julāḥ; al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād took it and would not give it back; Qays raided al-Rabīʿ's camels, sold them at Mecca and bought horses with the money, Dāḥis among them — and then his own mare foaled al-Ghabrāʾ. So the quarrel at the root of the war is about armour, not a horse. Then Qays matched his two against Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr's Khaṭṭār and Ḥanfāʾ over a course run across forty nights, for a stake of ten camels. Men hidden in the ravines turned the leading horse away from the finish. The loser refused to pay, the winner's kin were killed, and forty years of war followed in which neither tribe bred a camel or a horse.
events.dispute: Three incompatible versions of the race and two accounts of what caused the war. On the cause, the Arabic sources put something earlier than the race, which the usual retelling drops: Qays bought a coat of mail from Uḥayḥa ibn al-Julāḥ, al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād seized it and kept it, and Qays raided his camels, sold them at Mecca and bought the horses with the proceeds — so the origin is a mail-coat, not a horse. Both narrations should stand. On the race: in al-ʿIqd al-Farīd it is Ḥamal ibn Badr, not Ḥudhayfa, who hid the men, and Dāḥis is Qays's horse cheated of the win; in Ibn al-Athīr both Dāḥis and al-Ghabrāʾ are Qays's, a man of Banū Asad threw Dāḥis in the water and crippled his run, Ḥanfāʾ fell, and al-Ghabrāʾ came in ahead of Khaṭṭār — so the war's name pairs two horses that one source makes rivals and another makes stablemates. The escalation is doubled too: Ḥudhayfa's son Nadba, or his son Mālik, came to demand the stake and Qays killed him, after which the tribes agreed on a hundred she-camels in blood-money that al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād paid by himself. The whole war's conventional bracket of c. 568–609 is Muir's reconstruction, not a source date.

events.title: Ḥarrān inscription
events.dateNote: Fixed by the local era date: year 463 after the destruction of Khaybar, epoch c. 105 CE.
events.summary: A Greek-Arabic bilingual on the martyrium of St John, south of Damascus. Sharaḥīl son of Ṭalimu built it in 'year 463 after the destruction of Khaybar' — which means there was a local Arabian dating era running from a raid on an oasis around 105 CE.
events.dispute: The builder's patronym is read Ṭalimu in the publication, not Ẓālim as often reported.

sources.title: Harran Inscription: A Pre-Islamic Arabic Inscription From 568 CE

events.title: Yawm al-Ghadaq
events.dateNote: Undated; the year holds the day's place in al-ʿIqd al-Farīd's ordering.
events.summary: Called the first major clash of the war. Fazāra were routed and Ḥudhayfa himself was taken prisoner by al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād, and a man who tried to kill him there failed.
events.dispute: Undated; known only from the almerja text of Ibn al-Athīr.

events.title: Death of al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala
events.summary: Forty years a king, a patrikios, a Miaphysite kingmaker and the victor of Ḥalīma, he died during a reported earthquake. His son al-Mundhir took over and lasted twelve years.

events.title: The Letter of the Archimandrites
events.dateNote: The letter is dated 569 or 570.
events.summary: A conference the Ghassanids convened produced a letter signed by representatives of a hundred and thirty-seven monasteries. The measure of what an Arab client kingdom's church patronage actually amounted to.

events.title: Ṭarafa carries his own death warrant
events.dateNote: Placed c. 569 inside ʿAmr ibn Hind's reign; the episode is akhbār grown around the poems.
events.summary: He mocked the king in verse. ʿAmr ibn Hind sent him and his uncle al-Mutalammis home, each with a sealed letter for the governor of Baḥrayn. Neither could read. Al-Mutalammis had a boy from al-Ḥīra open his, found it ordered him buried alive, threw it in a stream and told Ṭarafa to do the same — and Ṭarafa would not break a royal seal. He was about twenty-six.
events.dispute: Burial alive is one version among several. The whole episode is akhbār grown around the poems.

events.title: Mālik ibn Zuhayr killed at al-Luqāṭa
events.dateNote: Undated; placed by its position in the Dāḥis sequence.
events.summary: Qays's brother camped at al-Luqāṭa, was betrayed to Ḥudhayfa and killed. ʿAntara's elegy for him is one of the few things the early sources actually attribute to ʿAntara.
events.dispute: Undated. Terms of two hundred camels and four slaves were accepted for the death at one point, with hostages held — one of several interim settlements the war chewed through.

sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.title: ج6 - ص18 - كتاب العقد الفريد - حرب داحس والغبراء وهي من حروب قيس

events.title: The monasteries of Hind
events.dateNote: Dated only to the second half of the 6th century.
events.summary: Two monasteries at al-Ḥīra, of Hind the Elder and Hind the Younger, both built in the second half of the 6th century. Hind was a Kindite princess married to al-Mundhir III; she converted and founded hers in the capital while her husband did not convert.
events.dispute: The Lakhmid women called Hind — the Elder, the Younger, al-Ḥurqa — are repeatedly conflated in the tradition, and the sources call one Hind both daughter and granddaughter of al-Nuʿmān.

events.title: The Persians take Yemen
events.dateNote: The siege of Ṣanʿāʾ is dated 570 in the external record; one strand of the literature puts the Sasanian annexation at 575 or 578 instead.
events.summary: A small expedition under Wahrīz, sailing with at least eight ships of which two are said to have sunk, besieged Ṣanʿāʾ and ended Ethiopian rule. South Arabia became a Sasanian province, and the conquest is formally listed among the causes of the next Byzantine-Persian war.

events.title: Saṭīḥ's deathbed prophecy
events.dateNote: Undated. Placed at the traditional eve of Muḥammad's birth because that is where the narrative puts it, not where any source dates it.
events.summary: An earthquake toppled pillars in the Persian throne room, the sacred fire at Iṣṭakhr went out, Lake Sāwa sank, and the chief priest dreamed of camels leading Arabian horses across the Tigris. Khusraw sent for an Arab sage, and the Lakhmid king sent a Christian who rode to Syria to find Saṭīḥ — boneless, near death, his companion Shiqq already dead. Saṭīḥ said an Arab prophet would come, that Persian rule would pass to the Arabs, and that the number of fallen pillars was the number of kings left. Then he died.
events.dispute: Savran reads Saṭīḥ and Shiqq as early-ʿAbbāsid literary constructions, 'connectors' inserted to tie ancient Arabia, the Sasanians and the rise of Islam into one master narrative, and legitimising agents making Jāhiliyya Arabs carry a hidden monotheist current. Al-Masʿūdī and Ibn Durayd put the Persian omens under Khusraw II instead of Khusraw I. The isnād of the main report is spurious. Using these two as 6th-century characters reproduces an ʿAbbāsid ideology rather than a 6th-century reality.

events.title: Yawm Ṭikhfa
events.dateNote: Undated, and the sources disagree over which Lakhmid king - father or son - fought there.
events.summary: Banū Yarbūʿ beat a Lakhmid king's force.
events.dispute: Which king is contested: al-Qalqashandī's list says Qābūs ibn al-Mundhir, Fajernet says al-Mundhir ibn Māʾ al-Samāʾ — father or son. Spelled Ṭikhfa in Ibn al-Athīr's contents and Ṭaḥfa in al-ʿIqd al-Farīd's. Undated.

events.title: The Year of the Elephant
events.dateNote: Contested in five directions across 552-572. The traditional 570-571 is a synchronism built to anchor a birth, and the one dated Abraha campaign northward, Ry 506 of 552, does not name Mecca.
events.summary: The tradition says Abraha marched north on Mecca with war elephants, took the Ṭāʾif road, lost a guide near al-Mughammas, and was turned back. The same year is given for Muḥammad's birth, and Meccan chronology is reckoned from it.
events.dispute: Contested in at least five directions: the traditional c. 570–571; 568 or 569 from South Arabian finds; 552 on the strength of Ry 506, which Gajda accepts and which does not mention Mecca; 'one or two decades earlier than 570'; and 14 February 572, proposed by Zein and el-Wakil. The Arabic sources add a support the English ones do not carry — al-Masʿūdī puts the expedition in the year corresponding to the fortieth of Khusraw Anūshirwān's reign, that is 571 — and al-Zuhrī, transmitted by ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī, has a tradition placing it before Muḥammad's father was born, which contradicts the 570 birth synchronism from inside the tradition. Abraha's epigraphic record stops at 559/560. A gap in the Arabic reference literature has to be stated here: the general Arabic works do not name CIH 541, do not mention the Murayghān inscriptions, and do not mention the year 552 at all — so the whole epigraphic side of the Year of the Elephant question is absent from the common Arabic reference shelf, and a reader working in Arabic has to go to DASI for it.

events.title: Muḥammad born at Mecca
events.dateNote: Pegged to the Year of the Elephant, which this atlas dates across 552-572, so the birth year inherits that whole spread; 570 is the conventional synchronism, not a transmitted date.
events.summary: A posthumous son of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, of the Banū Hāshim of Quraysh, born at Mecca. The traditional birthday is 12 Rabīʿ al-Awwal, with 17 Rabīʿ al-Awwal also given. Meccan chronology is reckoned forward from this year, which is why the uncertainty in it propagates through everything dated by his age.
events.dispute: The year rests on a synchronism with the Year of the Elephant, and that event is contested in five directions across 552-572 — including 552 on the strength of Ry 506, which does not mention Mecca, and al-Zuhrī's tradition placing the Elephant before ʿAbd Allāh was born, which contradicts the birth synchronism from inside the tradition. There is no inscriptional, archaeological or external documentary evidence for Mecca or Quraysh before 632; the whole Meccan record is literary and was written down about a century and a half later.

events.title: ʿAbd Allāh dies before his son is born
events.ar: وفاة عبد الله بن عبد المطلب
events.dateNote: Dated only relative to the birth — about six months before it — so the year moves with a birth year that is itself contested across 552-572.
