events.summary: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib died away from Mecca on a trading journey, leaving Āmina bint Wahb pregnant. The child was born into his grandfather's household rather than his father's.
events.dispute: No source dates the death independently; it is told as a measured interval before the birth. Al-Zuhrī's tradition putting the Year of the Elephant before ʿAbd Allāh was born cannot be reconciled with the standard scheme that makes the Elephant year the birth year.

events.title: Yawm al-Muraqqab
events.dateNote: An index entry with no narrative and no date; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: First day in the only ordered day-list the sources give for this war: ʿAbs over Fazāra.
events.dispute: An index entry with no narrative recovered. Undated.

sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.title: ج6 - ص18 - كتاب العقد الفريد - حرب داحس والغبراء وهي من حروب قيس

events.title: Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan rules as Persia's vassal
events.dateNote: His rule is given as 571-575, and the killing as 575 or 578.
events.summary: The Ḥimyarite heir who had gone begging first to Byzantium, then to al-Ḥīra, then to Khusraw's own court came home as a king who owed tribute. He was stabbed to death by an Abyssinian servant.
events.dispute: Death given as 575 or 578. There is also a chronological problem on the record: he is said to have been brokered by the Lakhmid al-Nuʿmān III, whose reign begins after Sayf's death.

events.title: The dam is left unrepaired
events.dateNote: Given as 570 or 575, with no source behind either figure.
events.summary: The barrage was overtopped and this time nobody fixed it. What the inscriptions show is not one catastrophic flood but a six-hundred-year maintenance cycle ending in the collapse of the political capacity to repair — exactly as Yemen changed hands from Aksum to Persia.
events.dispute: Given as 570 or 575 with no source for either figure. The Qurʾān's flood of the dam is read against this, though some scholars tie the scriptural passage to a breach around 145 BCE instead. The often-quoted figure of up to 50,000 migrants is flagged as uncited and should not be reported as fact.

events.title: Justin II orders a Ghassanid king killed
events.summary: The emperor ordered al-Mundhir assassinated. Al-Mundhir found out, and broke with the empire his father had served for forty years.

events.title: Yawm Dhū Ḥusā
events.dateNote: An index entry with no narrative and no date; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: Dhubyān over ʿAbs — the one clear ʿAbs defeat in the sequence, and still being thrown at them in verse after al-Habāʾa.
events.dispute: An index entry with no narrative recovered. Undated.

sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.title: ج6 - ص18 - كتاب العقد الفريد - حرب داحس والغبراء وهي من حروب قيس

events.title: Yawm al-Yaʿmariyya
events.dateNote: An index entry with no narrative, no location and no date; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: An ʿAbs win sitting between Dhū Ḥusā and al-Habāʾa. It is missing from most popular lists of the war entirely.
events.dispute: An index entry with no narrative recovered, and no location given. Undated.

events.title: The Ghassanids sack al-Ḥīra
events.summary: In the same year they were reconciled with Constantinople, the Ghassanids burned the Lakhmid capital.

events.title: Reconciliation at Sergiopolis
events.dateNote: Dated 575 in the Greek record; the Ruṣāfa inscription itself is undated.
events.summary: Three years of estrangement ended at the shrine of St Sergius in the desert, brokered by a Byzantine general. Al-Mundhir commissioned a building there, which a Greek inscription still identifies.
events.dispute: The Ruṣāfa inscription itself is undated in every source reached.

events.title: Yawm al-Habāʾa
events.dateNote: Undated; the year holds the day's place in al-ʿIqd al-Farīd's ordering.
events.summary: They met in summer heat beside the well, fought from morning to midday, and the heat parted them. Ḥudhayfa, suffering in his thighs, fell back to the water as Qays had predicted, and ʿAbs followed the hoofprints. Ḥamal asked his men whom they would least like to see coming; they named Qays and al-Rabīʿ, and those were the two who came. Ḥamal begged by God and by kinship and Qays refused, answering their cries for help with a taunting 'here I am' — an echo of children who had called out as they were killed. A broad-bladed spear broke the spine, and swords finished it. About four hundred dead on the Dhubyān side against twenty of ʿAbs. Fazāra called the day the Perdition instead.
events.dispute: Undated. The ʿIqd al-Farīd text does not name the man killed; two almerja texts state directly that Qarāwash ibn ʿAmr killed Ḥudhayfa and that his brother Ḥamal and his son died there too. The mutilation of the body is reported as a return of what he had done to boys earlier.

sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.title: ج6 - ص23 - كتاب العقد الفريد - يوم الهباءة لعبس على ذبيان

events.title: Wahrīz comes back with four thousand men
events.dateNote: Dated 575 or 578; the sources do not choose.
events.summary: After the vassal king was murdered the Persian general returned, cleared the Ethiopians out for good, and ruled as governor himself, installing Sayf's son as a figurehead.
events.dispute: Dated 575 or 578; the sources do not choose.

events.title: Āmina bint Wahb dies
events.dateNote: Counted as her son's sixth year, so the year moves with a birth placed anywhere in 552-572.
events.summary: Āmina died when her son was about six, leaving him an orphan on both sides. The tradition has her die on the road back from a visit to her late husband's kin at Yathrib.
events.dispute: Dated only by the boy's age. Nothing external touches her at all.

events.title: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's guardianship, then Abū Ṭālib's
events.ar: كفالة عبد المطلب ثم أبي طالب
events.dateNote: A two-year span counted as the boy's sixth to eighth years, so it slides with a birth placed anywhere in 552-572; no source dates ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's own floruit at all.
events.summary: The orphan passed to his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, head of the Banū Hāshim, and on the old man's death about two years later to his uncle Abū Ṭālib. That transfer is what put him under Hāshimī protection for the next forty years, and the protection is the thing the Meccan opposition later had to work around.
events.dispute: Both the span and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's death are arithmetic off the contested birth year. The research found no date at all for ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's floruit, and the Meccan genealogical chronology behind him is internally contradictory by a full century.

events.title: Death of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī
events.dateNote: The 578 date is from Kitāb al-Aghānī alone, and another tradition puts his death in the year of Muḥammad's birth.
events.summary: The chief of Ṭayyiʾ who gave away everything but his mount and his weapons died and was buried near Ḥāʾil. 'More generous than Ḥātim' is still a living proverb. Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih counted him one of the three most generous men of the Jāhiliyya, with Kaʿb ibn Māma and Harim ibn Sinān.
events.dispute: The 578 date comes from Kitāb al-Aghānī alone. Another tradition puts his death in the year of Muḥammad's birth, and d'Herbelot reports the tomb somewhere else entirely. No birth date exists.

events.title: ʿAdī ibn Zayd's embassy to Constantinople
events.dateNote: A court record under Hormizd IV. The year is transmitted by the Arabic tradition, not checked externally.
events.summary: The Sasanian king sent his Arab-affairs secretary — a Nestorian Christian of al-Ḥīra, raised at the Persian court, fluent in Arabic and Persian and probably Syriac — to the Byzantine capital. He came back with books.

events.title: Yawm al-Farūq
events.dateNote: Undated, and al-Khāqānī files al-Farūq as a Qays-against-Tamīm day instead; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: ʿAbs defeated a Kindite leader and the people of Hajar.
events.dispute: Al-Khāqānī's list instead makes al-Farūq a Qays-against-Tamīm day, which conflicts with reading it inside the Dāḥis cycle. The name has probably been reused for more than one engagement. Undated.

events.title: Yawm Raḥraḥān
events.dateNote: Undated; placed about a year before Shiʿb Jabala, which is the only link the sources give.
events.summary: Banū ʿĀmir and a Lakhmid column came to the nearest waters of Banū Dārim. A woman who saw the armies told Zurāra who the commanders were, and he got his family and herds away. Banū ʿĀmir took his son Maʿbad, who stayed their prisoner until he died — which is the whole reason for the war that followed.
events.dispute: Undated; placed here only because it is said to be about a year before Shiʿb Jabala. The victor is contested: Ibn al-Athīr has Banū ʿĀmir and the Lakhmids routed when Qays ibn Zuhayr arrived, al-ʿIqd al-Farīd's index tags the day for ʿĀmir over Tamīm, and al-Qalqashandī's list suggests the name covers two engagements.

events.title: Yawm al-Waqīṭ
events.dateNote: Undated and unlocated; the year is a placement inside the period.
events.summary: Bakr of Rabīʿa over Tamīm. Al-ʿIqd al-Farīd heads a whole cluster of Bakr-over-Tamīm days with it.
events.dispute: Undated and unlocated. Fajernet gives the tribes without naming a winner.

events.title: Yawm Shiʿb Jabala
events.dateNote: A spread of about sixty years once both Arabic reckonings are admitted - 551, 553, al-ʿIqd al-Farīd's 'forty years before Islam, the year the Prophet was born' which is c. 570, al-Khāqānī's 'fifty-seven years before Islam' which is c. 565, Caskel's c. 580 and Bosworth's 582-602 - and only c. 580 fits al-Mundhir IV being among the leaders.
events.summary: Laqīṭ ibn Zurāra called in his allies to avenge his brother: all of Ghaṭafān answered except the Banū Badr, all of Tamīm except the Banū Saʿd, the Banū Asad came in on an old pact, al-Jawn al-Kalbī king of Hajar sent his two sons Muʿāwiya and ʿAmr, and al-Nuʿmān sent his half-brother Ḥassān ibn Barra. The muster was set for the turn of the year from Yawm Raḥraḥān. ʿĀmir and ʿAbs took the blind pass on Qays ibn Zuhayr's advice, moved their women and goods inside, and left the camels hobbled, unwatered and unfed for twelve nights. Then they cut the hobbles. The herd's roar in the gorge made the besiegers think the mountain had come down on them, and the footmen came out holding the camels' tails, and the horse behind the footmen. Laqīṭ was killed; Ḥājib ibn Zurāra was taken, and Sinān ibn Abī Ḥāritha, whose forelock ʿUrwa al-Raḥḥāl cut before letting him go, and ʿAmr ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUdus. Kindite power in northern Arabia was finished.
events.dispute: The field's best demonstration of how bad the chronology is. The two oldest Arabic sources give different counts of years before Islam and the English version carried only the second: al-ʿIqd al-Farīd says 'forty years before Islam, and it is the year in which the Prophet was born', which is about 570 and is the most widely repeated figure, while al-Khāqānī's list says 'fifty-seven years before Islam', about 565. With 551, 553, Caskel's c. 580 and Bosworth's placement under al-Nuʿmān III (582–602), the spread for one famous battle runs to roughly sixty years rather than fifty. Worse, the data contradict most of the options: al-Mundhir IV (r. 575–580) among the leaders fits Caskel's c. 580 and nothing else. And the Arabic text contradicts itself inside one passage — al-ʿIqd al-Farīd dates the day to about 570 and then names among its commanders al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir (580–602), who sent his half-brother Ḥassān ibn Barra, a king who did not reign until ten years later. Recommended handling: c. 580 internally, with 570 as the folk date characters cite, since 570 is exactly what al-ʿIqd al-Farīd says.

events.title: Yawm Qaṭan
events.dateNote: An index entry with no narrative, no location and no date; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: A day in the Dāḥis sequence known only from the ordered index.
events.dispute: Index entry only: no narrative, no location, no date.

events.title: Yawm Dhū Najab
events.dateNote: Dated only as one year after Shiʿb Jabala, per al-Khāqānī. That relative link is firmer than either absolute date.
events.summary: A year after Shiʿb Jabala the Yarbūʿ clan of Tamīm took their revenge, killed Ibn Kabsha and cut up several Kilābī chiefs.
events.dispute: Dated only relative to Shiʿb Jabala — one year after, per al-Khāqānī, who gives Jabala as 57 years before Islam. That relative link is firmer than either absolute date.

events.title: Al-Nuʿmān III at al-Ḥīra
events.dateNote: Given as both 580 and 582 inside a single reference article; 581 is a midpoint of the two, and endYear carries the reign to the fixed 602 deposition rather than to the 595 one passage of the same article gives.
events.summary: The last Lakhmid king took the throne. He converted openly to Nestorian Christianity, probably after the peace of 591, and al-Ḥīra became a major church centre with a bishopric and missions down the Gulf.
events.dispute: His accession is given as both 580 and 582 inside a single reference article, and his reign end as 595 in one passage and 602 in another.

events.title: Al-Mundhir arrested and exiled to Sicily
events.dateNote: Dated 581 in one place and 582 in another.
events.summary: After a failed campaign on Ctesiphon, Maurice and al-Mundhir each blamed the other. Al-Mundhir was arrested, held in Constantinople, and sent to Sicily once Maurice was emperor. A 13th-century Syriac chronicle says he came home after Maurice fell in 602.
events.dispute: Dated 581 in one place and 582 in another, within the same cluster of sources.

events.title: Yawm Ghadīr Qalhā
events.dateNote: An index entry with no narrative, no location and no date; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: A day at a rain pool, known only from the ordered index.
events.dispute: Index entry only: no narrative, no location, no date.

sources.title: يوم قطن
sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.note: Yawm Ghadīr Qalhā is told on the same page, after Yawm Quṭn.
sources.noteAr: يومُ غدير قَلْهى مرويٌّ في الصفحة نفسها بعد يوم قطن.

events.title: The Ghassanid phylarchate breaks up
events.summary: Byzantium arrested al-Nuʿmān VI and tried him for treason, and the confederation came apart — split, one source says, into fifteen member tribes. Maurice is reported to have patched it back together two or three years later because the empire could not hold the desert without it.

events.title: Yawm al-Raqam
events.dateNote: Undated, and the day is not an ʿAbs-against-Dhubyān fight at all; the year only holds its place in the index.
events.summary: Ghaṭafān over Banū ʿĀmir.
events.dispute: Filed inside the Dāḥis cycle in the indexes but it is not an ʿAbs-against-Dhubyān day at all. Al-Khāqānī has it as Banū Fazāra against Banū ʿĀmir. Another reused name. Undated.

sources.author: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih
sources.title: ج6 - ص18 - كتاب العقد الفريد - حرب داحس والغبراء وهي من حروب قيس

events.title: Al-Barrāḍ breaks the sacred month
events.dateNote: The whole cycle is dated only by Muḥammad's reported age at it, given anywhere from 14 to 20.
events.summary: Al-Barrāḍ ibn Qays, a Kinānī man expelled by his own tribe, ambushed ʿUrwa al-Raḥḥāl of Banū ʿĀmir during a sacred month and seized the Lakhmid king's caravan. That is the sacrilege the Fijār wars are named for.
events.dispute: Dated only by Muḥammad's reported age at the wars, given anywhere from 14 to 20, which puts the cycle in the 580s–590s. Landau-Tasseron reads the cause differently: Quraysh and ʿĀmir shared an interest in Lakhmid caravans, and al-Barrāḍ's branch was hostile to the Jaʿfar clan over a cancelled protection covenant.

events.title: Yawm Nakhla
events.dateNote: Undated. The order of the eight days is firmer than any of their years.
events.summary: Hawāzin fell on Quraysh and Kināna, who got away into the sanctuary at nightfall. Usually counted the fourth day of the Fijār, after three brawls that the sources count sometimes as one war and sometimes as three.
events.dispute: Undated. The order of the eight days is firmer than any of their years.

events.title: Yawm ʿArāʿir
events.dateNote: Undated, and the two mirrors of the same source disagree about which tribe lost; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: Masʿūd ibn Miṣād, chief of Kalb, was killed here and Kalb routed.
events.dispute: One almerja text says that; the mirror of the same text says Fazāra fought ʿAbs here and Fazāra won. The identity of the losing tribe at ʿArāʿir is genuinely contested. Undated.

events.title: Yawm Shamṭa
events.dateNote: Undated. The order of the eight days is firmer than any of their years.
events.summary: A Fijār day near ʿUkāẓ the following year. Hawāzin won.
events.dispute: Undated.

events.title: Yawm al-ʿAblāʾ
events.dateNote: Undated. The order of the eight days is firmer than any of their years.
events.summary: Fighting at the fairground itself. Hawāzin won again.
events.dispute: Undated.

events.title: Yawm ʿUkāẓ
events.dateNote: Undated. The order of the eight days is firmer than any of their years.
events.summary: Also called Yawm Sharab. The one day of the whole cycle that Quraysh and Kināna won.
events.dispute: Undated.

events.title: Yawm Dhāt al-Jarājir
events.dateNote: Undated and unlocated; the year holds its place in the sequence.
events.summary: Two consecutive days of fighting between ʿAbs and Dhubyān, and the one day on which the sources specifically single out ʿAntara's courage.
events.dispute: Undated, and no location given. The sources are notably sparse on ʿAntara generally: he is attested composing an elegy for Mālik ibn Zuhayr and as the hero of this day, and that is nearly all.

events.title: Yawm al-Ḥurayra and the peace
events.dateNote: Al-Khāqānī's list gives 589 for the end of Fijār II - the only CE date anywhere in the minor-days corpus for this cycle.
events.summary: The eighth and last day, on the lava field near ʿUkāẓ, won by Hawāzin. A few skirmishes and then peace. Hawāzin had taken four days, Quraysh one, and the rest were brawls.
events.dispute: Al-Khāqānī's list gives 589 as the end of Fijār II — the single CE date anywhere in the minor-days corpus for this cycle. Everything else is dated off Muḥammad's age.

events.title: Al-Nuʿmān III shelters a fugitive king
events.dateNote: The flight and the fighting at al-Nahrawān run across 590-591.
events.summary: Khusraw II, driven out by the usurper Bahrām Chōbīn, was sheltered by the Lakhmid king and fought beside him at al-Nahrawān. Maurice backed the restoration. Twelve years later Khusraw destroyed him.

events.title: Yawm al-Sullān II, also Qāʿ al-Qurayṭayn
events.ar: يوم السلان الثاني (قاع القُرَيتَين / يوم السُّوبان)
events.dateNote: Undated; the window is al-Nuʿmān III's reign.
events.summary: Banū ʿĀmir seized the trading caravan al-Nuʿmān sent to ʿUkāẓ every year, so he raised an army under his half-brother Wabra and the clans of Tamīm. Quraysh got word and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān warned Banū ʿĀmir, who were ready. Wabra was captured in the charge and the army broke. The old man Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr forbade his men to flee and held the command with his sons shielding him while Abū Barāʾ knocked him down again and again. Abū Barāʾ asked him to point out a man worth ransoming; Ḍirār pointed to Ḥubaysh ibn Dalaf, who was thin and black and looked like a slave, so Abū Barāʾ thought he had been tricked — and Ḥubaysh ransomed himself for four hundred camels. Wabra went for a thousand camels and a horse, which made his captor rich.
events.dispute: Three names for one day: al-Sullān II, Yawm al-Sūbān, and Qāʿ al-Qurayṭayn. The Arabic sources confirm the third, which resolves the otherwise unidentified 'Yawm al-Qurnatayn' — it is Qāʿ al-Qurayṭayn, an alternative name for this day, so no separate battle needs to be posited. Undated; the window is al-Nuʿmān III's reign. The Arabic criticism of the secondary literature belongs here: Jawād ʿAlī confused the two Sullāns and tied Khazāz to this one, so dated Khazāz to al-Nuʿmān's time, which is a serious error; al-Maydānī confused them too, putting ʿĀmir's title 'Mulāʿib al-Asinna' at al-Sullān I when it was earned here, and assigning to al-Sullān a verse of Zuhayr ibn Janāb that belongs to Khazāz.

sources.title: مدونة محمد مفرج السيد الرديني : السلان ( يوم السلان )

events.title: The treaty of 591
events.summary: Khusraw II returned Dara and Martyropolis and the Caucasus was repartitioned — and for the first time Byzantium paid nothing at all. A real shift in the balance between the two empires, and the last peace before the war that ruined both.

events.title: Al-Nuʿmān III converts
events.dateNote: Dated only by inference from the 591 peace.
events.summary: The last Lakhmid king became the first of his line to convert openly to Nestorian Christianity, probably after the peace of 591, with the bishop of al-Ḥīra instrumental. The Persians disapproved and tried to make him go back.
events.dispute: Dated only by inference from the 591 peace. One tradition instead makes Imruʾ al-Qays I the first Lakhmid convert, centuries earlier.

events.title: Ḥilf al-Fuḍūl
events.dateNote: Undated in every source reached, and the causal chain from the Fijār that would date it is unverified.
events.summary: A compact among Meccan clans to stand up for the wronged man against his own kin's interest, sworn after an incident over a cheated outsider.
events.dispute: Undated in every source reached, and the Fijār article does not connect the two, so any causal chain from the Fijār to this oath is unverified. The clans conventionally named — Hāshim, Zuhra, Asad, Taym, al-Muṭṭalib — are not confirmed by anything accessible.

events.title: Marriage to Khadīja bint Khuwaylid
events.dateNote: Counted as his twenty-fifth year, so the conventional c. 595 slides with a birth placed anywhere in 552-572.
events.summary: Khadīja bint Khuwaylid, a twice-widowed Qurashī businesswoman of the Banū Asad who financed caravans, employed him on a Syrian journey and then married him. She was about forty by the tradition's reckoning and he about twenty-five. He took no other wife while she lived, and her money and standing are what freed him from working for a living.
events.dispute: Dated only by his age. Her commercial role is repeated in every sīra account and examined in none: the searches turned up only devotional and popular treatments, no critical scholarship on whether a woman financing Meccan caravans is historically plausible.

events.title: ʿAdī ibn Zayd strangled
events.dateNote: Placed c. 600, before al-Nuʿmān III's own fall in 602.
events.summary: Al-Nuʿmān III had his chief councillor imprisoned and strangled on suspicion of plotting. ʿAdī's son had Khusraw's ear, and the killing is believed to have poisoned Sasanian-Lakhmid relations and helped bring the dynasty down. The third poet al-Ḥīra killed in forty-five years.

events.title: Yawm al-Ṣafqa and al-Mushaqqar
events.dateNote: Undated in every source; the Arabic narrative fixes what happened without fixing when. Its only chronological handle is the Sasanian frame, Khusraw Parvīz's reign.
events.summary: Tamīm raided a caravan of Khusraw's and robbed his envoys with it. The king called up Hawdha ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥanafī, his man in al-Yamāma, to punish them, and sent the Persian commander al-Mukaʿbir with a force of heavy cavalry. The two of them took the fortress of al-Mushaqqar in Hajar, and in a year of famine they put out word of grain for sale. The Tamīmīs were let in a few at a time and killed a few at a time. When it came out, a man of ʿAbs cut the chain off the door so that those standing at the gate got clear; al-Mukaʿbir shut the gates and killed everyone still inside. That shutting is the name — al-Ṣafqa, the closing. The day fell on Easter, so Hawdha asked for a hundred Tamīmī prisoners and let them go, and al-Aʿshā put it in a poem.
events.dispute: The English version found only a one-line gloss in al-Khāqānī's list and filed the day under what could not be recovered; Tawfīq Barrū's Tārīkh al-ʿArab al-Qadīm gives the full narrative summarised here, so the day is solved. A different version in the same source's footnote, from Jād al-Mawlā, inverts it: Tamīm ambushed Hawdha in a valley and held him until three hundred camels were paid for his release. Ibn al-Athīr and al-ʿIqd al-Farīd both pair the day in one chapter with Yawm al-Kulāb II. Still undated, and al-Mushaqqar itself is unlocated.

events.title: Harim ibn Sinān and al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf buy the peace
events.dateNote: The war's c. 568-609 bracket is Muir's reconstruction; no source dates the settlement.
events.summary: Two cousins of Murra, Harim ibn Sinān and al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf, went into the mediation together and paid the blood-price of the dead on both sides out of their own property — some three thousand camels, handed over across three years. Forty years of killing between ʿAbs and Dhubyān stopped. Zuhayr named them both in his Muʿallaqa for it. Qays ibn Zuhayr would not go with his tribe: he said he would not be a Ghaṭafānī, turned Christian, wandered as far as Oman and lived as a monk there until a man of ʿAbd al-Qays killed him.
events.dispute: The Arabic sources settle what the English reconstruction could not confirm and had marked unverified: Harim ibn Sinān and his cousin al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf entered the mediation together, carried the blood-money out of their own wealth at about three thousand camels over three years, and were praised by name in Zuhayr's Muʿallaqa for their stand on the war — figures, duration and amount all stated. The English version credited al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf alone, treated the Harim-blood-money-Muʿallaqa chain as unverified, and found Harim's father Sinān only as a failed coalition-builder on the opposing side; father and son on two sides of one matter is not a contradiction. The Arabic sources further correct the claim that Harim's brother Khārija carried the blood-money, which is not sound. Still undated: the war's conventional bracket of c. 568–609 is Sir William Muir's Victorian reconstruction, not a source date, and no source dates the settlement itself. Qays ibn Zuhayr's end is doubled — he went with ʿAbs to Dhubyān and the peace was made, or he refused, took the cross and died a monk's death in Oman.

sources.title: الحارث بن عوف المري
sources.note: Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf carried the blood-money of the Dāḥis war together with Harim ibn Sinān.
sources.noteAr: الحارث بن عوف أحدُ مَن حملوا دياتِ حرب داحس والغبراء مع هرم بن سنان.

sources.title: هرم بن سنان
sources.note: Harim ibn Sinān worked with al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf for peace between ʿAbs and Dhubyān and bore the blood-money.
sources.noteAr: سعى هرم بن سنان مع الحارث بن عوف في الصلح بين عبس وذبيان، وتحمّلا ديات القتلى.

events.title: Yawm al-Kulāb II and al-Ṣafqa
events.dateNote: Undated; placed late because Ibn al-Athīr pairs it in one chapter with Yawm al-Ṣafqa.
events.summary: Banū Tamīm against Banū al-Ḥārith and Madhḥij, with Khusraw Parvīz's deputy in the background and a Tamīmī raid on his envoys as the cause. Banū al-Ḥārith gathered on the advice of a soothsayer, and Madhḥij marched despite being told not to.
events.dispute: Ibn al-Athīr pairs it in one chapter with Yawm al-Ṣafqa, and so does al-ʿIqd al-Farīd. Fajernet calls it Tamīm against Banū ʿAbd al-Madān of Najrān; al-Khāqānī has Tamīm over Madhḥij. All three fit if ʿAbd al-Madān is a clan of Banū al-Ḥārith of Najrān allied with Madhḥij. The Arabic sources supply the Persian frame in detail — Khusraw Parvīz's deputy sent to Yemen, a Tamīmī raid on his envoys, and Hawdha ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥanafī rising in the king's regard for treating the robbed men well — which is the same chain that produces Yawm al-Ṣafqa. Undated.

sources.title: إسلام ويب  - الكامل في التاريخ - ذكر أيام العرب في الجاهلية - يوم الصفقة والكلاب الثاني- الجزء رقم1

events.title: Al-Nābigha comes back from exile
events.dateNote: Placed with ʿAdī ibn Zayd's killing, c. 600.
events.summary: The poet who had fled to the Ghassanids after verses about the queen returned to al-Ḥīra, and withdrew to his tribe when al-Nuʿmān fell. The one well-attested case of a poet shuttling between the two client courts.

events.title: Yawm al-Shaqīqa and the death of Bisṭām
events.dateNote: A chapter heading in Ibn al-Athīr's list with no narrative recovered and no date.
events.summary: The day on which the famous raider Bisṭām ibn Qays was killed.
events.dispute: A chapter heading in Ibn al-Athīr's list of days with no narrative recovered. Undated.

sources.title: يوم الشقيقة وقتل بسطام بن قيس
sources.author: Ibn al-Athīr, ed. ʿUmar ʿAbd al-Salām Tadmurī

events.title: Death of ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward
events.dateNote: Dates given as 520 and 600 with no apparatus behind either; c. 600 is the convention.
events.summary: The outlaw of ʿAbs who stole to feed the poor, and was called the most generous of the ancient Arabs. Some of his verse is about the wife he divorced while drunk and despaired over when sober.
events.dispute: Dates given as 520–600 with no apparatus behind either figure.

events.title: Khusraw II destroys the Lakhmid kingdom
events.summary: The king was deposed, seized at Ctesiphon, imprisoned at Khānaqīn, and died there of plague. Al-Ḥīra went to Iyās ibn Qabīṣa al-Ṭāʾī and the dynasty was over. In the same year Phocas murdered Maurice and Khusraw declared the war that ran to 628. The structural pivot of the whole period.
events.dispute: Two Syriac chronicles give rival accounts of his end, one a feast at which he was dishonoured and trapped, one a capture with his sons who were then poisoned. One tradition has him crushed by elephants. The Arabic sources blame his refusal to hand over a horse or a daughter; the likelier cause is the ʿAdī ibn Zayd affair.

events.title: Umayya and Nawfal break with the Perfumed
events.dateNote: The tradition gives a bare 605 for the split and there is nothing external to check it against; Mecca has no dated record at all before 632.
events.summary: The Banū Umayya and Banū Nawfal split from the al-Muṭayyabūn faction. One of only two usable fixed points in Meccan internal politics.

events.title: The Kaʿba rebuilt and the Black Stone arbitration
events.dateNote: Counted five years before the revelation in the usual reckoning, which anchors it to 610; the competing reckoning by his age of thirty-five ties it instead to the contested birth year and would widen the span by two decades.
events.summary: The Quraysh took the sanctuary down and rebuilt it, and the clans then fell out over who would set the Black Stone back in its corner. The settlement reported is that the stone was carried in a cloak whose edges the clan representatives held together, so that all of them placed it. Whatever happened, the story is about the Meccan habit of arbitration rather than about the building.
events.dispute: The year is derived, not transmitted — five years before the revelation in one reckoning, his thirty-fifth year in another, and the second makes it move with the contested birth. The veneration of a quadrangular stone at Mecca is independently plausible: Marinus of Tyre described Arabs venerating one in the 2nd century. But Robin argues the Kaʿba only rose to prominence in the late 6th century, and Webb argues it was a regional rather than a pan-Arabian pilgrimage site.

events.title: Yawm Dhū Qār
events.dateNote: Muslim tradition spreads it 602-624; the Arabic sources prefer 609 and give 604 as well, with late 609 or early 610 as the likeliest, and they reject the 624 end of the range outright. The 602 deposition is a hard lower bound because every account chains the battle to al-Nuʿmān's fall.
events.summary: Bakr ibn Wāʾil beat a Sasanian force with Ṭayyiʾ, Taghlib and Iyād auxiliaries at a desert watering place. The traditional figures are two thousand Persians and three thousand Arab allies. Leadership among the Bakr shifted from warrior to warrior with no commander-in-chief. It is remembered as the day the Arabs first beat the Persians.
events.dispute: Muslim tradition spreads it from 602 to 624; modern scholarship narrows it to 604–611, and the Arabic sources prefer 609, with late 609 or early 610 as the likeliest, al-Khāqānī's list saying only 'the year forty', near the Prophet's birth. The upper end is not merely awkward but refuted in the Arabic reference itself: al-Iṣfahānī's Aghānī reports that the battle fell some months after Badr and that the Prophet commented on it at Medina, no historian confirms it, and al-Albānī graded that hadith weak — so 624 is rejected on Arabic ground, as well as being impossible because every account chains the battle to the aftermath of al-Nuʿmān's deposition in 602. The site is disputed too: the Arabic sources put it at Ṭarīf, south of Medina in the north of the peninsula, not in southern Iraq near the modern Dhī Qār governorate, and the common placement is an inference from that modern province name. No source locates it definitively. Persian sources do not mention the battle at all, and Rezakhani holds it may have been no more than a skirmish — which makes its fame retrospective, and dramatically more interesting, not less. The Arabic sources add that Iyād withdrew under a secret agreement with Bakr, and count the forces as about three thousand Arabs, a thousand Persian asāwira and a thousand khanābirīn. Al-Nuʿmān III was not killed in or just before the battle: he was deposed in 602, taken to Ctesiphon, held at Khānaqīn and died, most likely of plague.

events.title: Death of ʿAntara
events.dateNote: The traditional 608 sits alongside 615 and al-Ziriklī's 600 inside a single Arabic article, and alongside versions that kill him in the Dāḥis fighting decades earlier or have him die of old age.
events.summary: The slave-born ʿAbsī warrior-poet died of a wound taken on a raid he led as an old man against the Banū Nabhān of Ṭayyiʾ — shot by Zurr ibn Jābir al-Nabhānī, carried home, dead among his own people. Eighty-two or eighty-three by the traditional reckoning, about ninety by another line of the same page.
events.dispute: Mutually exclusive versions, and the Arabic sources both prefer one and correct a name. Their preferred account, from Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī: as an old man he raided the Banū Nabhān of Ṭayyiʾ and drove off a herd, was shot by Zurr ibn Jābir al-Nabhānī, and went home wounded and died there. Ibn al-Kalbī reports that the killer was nicknamed al-Asad al-Rahīṣ al-Ṭāʾī. The name in the English sources, 'Wasr ibn Jābir', is wrong; it is Zurr. The rival versions — killed in the Dāḥis fighting, or dead of old age on Abū ʿUbayda's account — survive, but the first contradicts the 608 date held in the same corpus. The year itself is unstable inside one Arabic article: 608 in its lead, a life of 525–615 in its death section, and 600 from al-Ziriklī, with the page saying he reached about ninety and the infobox saying he died at eighty-three.

events.title: Death of Quss ibn Sāʿida
events.dateNote: c. 610 is a convention; a reported lifespan of 380, 600 or 700 years shows how little is behind it.
events.summary: The preacher who stood up in the market at ʿUkāẓ and spoke rhymed prose about one God and the resurrection died and was buried, probably in north Syria. One sermon survives, opening 'O People! Listen and retain!'
events.dispute: He is considered legendary or semi-legendary and is known only from Muslim sources. His lifespan is given as 380, 600 or 700 years, which is the clearest possible marker of legendary accretion. He is also called a bishop of Najrān in some accounts and a pagan sage in others.

events.title: Taʾabbaṭa Sharran killed on a raid
events.dateNote: His dates are explicitly unknown; late 6th or early 7th century is inferred from personal names in the poems.
events.summary: Killed raiding Banū Hudhayl, his body thrown into a cave called al-Rakhmān. His dīwān runs to two hundred and thirty-eight verses in thirty-two pieces.
events.dispute: His dates are explicitly unknown; late 6th or early 7th century is inferred from personal names in the poems. The nickname has three mutually exclusive explanations in Kitāb al-Aghānī alone — he carried a ram that turned out to be a ghūl, he filled his mother's truffle-bag with snakes, or he carried his sword under his arm — and modern scholars say none should be taken at face value.

events.title: The revelation begins at Ḥirāʾ
events.dateNote: Twelve years before the Hijra in the standard reckoning, which is counted from a fixed epoch; the traditional age of forty would instead tie the same moment to the contested birth year.
events.summary: On a retreat in a cave on Jabal al-Nūr outside Mecca, Muḥammad reported an encounter and a command to recite. The tradition has him go home shaken, Khadīja accept the account, and her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal — named among the pre-Islamic Arab monotheists — identify it in terms drawn from the earlier scriptures. Preaching stayed private for about three years.
events.dispute: The whole episode is sīra narrative. Being dated in years before the Hijra makes it firmer than anything reckoned by his age, but nothing external touches it, and the sources disagree about where other early episodes such as the night journey belong in the sequence.

events.title: Al-Khansāʾ loses her brothers
events.dateNote: Muʿāwiya's death is dated 612-613 and Ṣakhr's is inferred as about a year later.
events.summary: Her brother Muʿāwiya was killed in Banū Sulaym's skirmishes with Murra and Asad. Her brother Ṣakhr avenged him and died of his wounds about a year later. Over a hundred elegies for those two deaths survive, nearly a thousand lines.
events.dispute: Ṣakhr's death is inferred as 'about a year later'. Al-Khansāʾ herself has no birth or death date in any accessible source.

events.title: The daʿwa goes public
events.dateNote: Nine years before the Hijra in the standard reckoning; the figure is a round interval in the tradition rather than a dated event.
events.summary: After about three years of private preaching Muḥammad began addressing Mecca openly, calling for one God and warning of a judgement. The message bore directly on the sanctuary the Quraysh kept and on the gods whose shrines drew tribes from across the Ḥijāz, and organised Qurashī opposition dates from here.
events.dispute: A round three-year interval after the first revelation, which is how the tradition structures the period rather than how it dates it. Nothing external.

events.title: Jerusalem falls and the Cross goes east
events.summary: Three weeks of siege, then the city, then the True Cross carried off to Ctesiphon. The whole Christian East felt this one.

events.title: Migrations to Aksum
events.dateNote: Counted in years before the Hijra, but the sources give the first group 7 BH (615) or 9 BH (613) and the second 6 BH (616) or 7 BH (615), and some accounts date the first departure only to 'Rajab of the fifth year after the mission'.
events.summary: Groups of Muḥammad's followers crossed the Red Sea to Christian Aksum and were given asylum by the ruler the Arabic sources call al-Najāshī, the Negus. A Qurashī delegation is said to have gone after them and been refused. Mecca's trouble with its own preacher thereby entered the Red Sea politics that Aksum and Ḥimyar had been fighting over for a century — and the refugees from Najrān had taken the same route to the same court ninety years earlier.
events.dispute: Caetani and Watt doubted there were two distinct migrations at all; Watt read Ibn Isḥāq's wording as smaller groups arriving one after another, and traced the two canonical lists to later disputes over precedence in the registers under ʿUmar. The Negus cannot be matched to the Aksumite king-list with confidence: the identification with Armah dates from 1895, Ella Tsaham is the alternative, and Hahn has argued Armah was a son of Kāleb under another name.

events.title: The boycott of the Banū Hāshim
events.dateNote: A span counted in years before the Hijra, roughly 7 BH to 3 BH; the tradition gives it as about three years rather than as dated start and end.
events.summary: Qurashī clans agreed to break off marriage and trade with the Banū Hāshim and the Banū al-Muṭṭalib, who withdrew to a shiʿb, a defile on the edge of the town. It was a sanctions regime against a clan that would not surrender one of its own, not a siege: the mechanism being used was the ordinary one of clan protection, which is why the boycott had to be aimed at the whole clan rather than at the man. It broke down after about three years.
events.dispute: Dated only as an interval before the Hijra, with the beginning given as c. 616 and the lifting as 619. The document said to have been hung in the Kaʿba, and the story of its being eaten away, are narrative detail with nothing external behind them.

events.title: Yawm Buʿāth
events.dateNote: Counted back from the Hijra, which is the one fixed point the Arabic tradition really has.
events.summary: Aws, backed by the Jewish Qurayẓa and Naḍīr, beat Khazraj, backed by Qaynuqāʿ. The Khazraj chief ʿAmr ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Bayāḍī had seized hostages from the Jewish tribes and killed them, which is what drove those tribes to the other side. He was killed in the fighting. Afterwards the two exhausted tribes chose ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy to keep the peace — and the vacancy his weakness left is the one Muḥammad walked into in 622.
events.dispute: Dated by counting back from the Hijra, which is the one fixed point the Arabic tradition really has. One reference article calls the day inconclusive while another says the Aws won.

events.title: Alexandria falls
events.dateNote: The year-long siege ends 619 in the usual reckoning; the Greek chronology allows 618-620.
events.summary: Egypt went after a year-long siege, and the grain dole at Constantinople was abolished. Plague followed.

events.title: The Year of Sorrow: Khadīja and Abū Ṭālib die
events.dateNote: Three years before the Hijra in the standard reckoning; the year is given as 619 or 620 and the two deaths are placed within months of each other without either being dated.
events.summary: Khadīja and Abū Ṭālib died in the same year, shortly after the boycott ended. The second death mattered politically as much as the first mattered personally: Abū Ṭālib had held the Hāshimī protection over his nephew, and his successor as clan head did not. Within two years Muḥammad was looking for a tribe outside Mecca to take him in.
events.dispute: Neither death carries a date of its own. The sequence — boycott ends, protector dies, search for an outside ally — is the tradition's own causal chain, and it is sounder as a sequence than as a chronology.

events.title: Musaylima claims prophethood in the Falj
events.dateNote: Placed only as 'before the Hijra'.
events.summary: A Ḥanīfa soothsayer in his village of Haddār, in the Falj valley, declared himself a prophet before the Hijra. Central Arabia produced its own claimants, and the Yamāma was settled farming country with its own religious life.

events.title: The first pledge at al-ʿAqaba
events.dateNote: One year before the Hijra in the standard reckoning, at a pilgrimage season; no calendar date.
events.summary: Twelve men of Yathrib, mostly Khazraj, met Muḥammad at al-ʿAqaba near Minā during the pilgrimage and undertook to follow him. Yathrib had come out of Yawm Buʿāth four years earlier with its two Arab tribes exhausted and a consensus leader whose authority was thin, and the oasis was looking for an arbitrator from outside — which is the opening these meetings exploit.
events.dispute: The whole negotiation is sīra material, dated only by its position relative to the Hijra and the pilgrimage calendar.

events.title: The Hijra
events.dateNote: The epoch of the Hijrī calendar, from which the rest of the Arabic chronology is counted; the tradition places the arrival at Yathrib in September 622.
events.summary: Muḥammad moved from Mecca to Yathrib with the followers who had not already gone, after oaths taken at al-ʿAqaba in the two previous pilgrimage seasons; the tradition puts the arrival in September. The year became the epoch of the Islamic calendar, which is why so much of the Arabian chronology in this atlas is counted backwards from it.
events.dispute: The year is the epoch of the Hijrī calendar and so the one date in the Arabic tradition not reckoned off something else — but it is not fixed by anything external either, and the earliest Greek and Syriac notices of the Arabs begin later. The event is attested only in the later Arabic tradition, which is why it is graded TRAD here even though the year itself is not in doubt. Heraclius leaving Constantinople in the same year is a separate, Byzantine-sourced event and is listed on its own.

events.title: Heraclius opens the counteroffensive
events.dateNote: Dated in the Byzantine record to 4 April 622.
events.summary: Heraclius left Constantinople on 4 April to begin the campaign that would break Persia within six years. It falls in the same year as the Hijra, months apart, and the two together close the period this atlas covers: the empire that had fought Persia to exhaustion was about to meet a power that had not existed when the war began.
events.dispute: Independent of the Hijra and sourced separately. The two were previously carried as a single entry here, which left one source link standing for two unrelated events.

events.title: The second pledge at al-ʿAqaba
events.dateNote: Placed in June 622, months before the move to Yathrib; the year is firm because it is the Hijra year itself, the month is tradition.
events.summary: A much larger party from Yathrib — seventy-three men and two women of both Aws and Khazraj by the usual count — pledged at the same place, this time undertaking to defend him. The emigration followed within months.
events.dispute: The numbers and the terms come from the sīra. The timing is the firmest thing about it, because it sits immediately before the one date the Arabic tradition really has.

events.title: Heraclius in the Persian heartland
events.summary: He sacked Dvin and beat Khusraw's army at Ganzaka with help from loyal Arabs — the Arab clients fighting in an imperial war as both empires ran out of men.

events.title: Battle of Nineveh
events.summary: On 12 December Heraclius broke the Persian army and then plundered Dastagird. Within a year Khusraw II was dead and his son was suing for peace.

events.title: Bādhān, last Persian governor of Yemen
events.summary: The last Sasanian governor in South Arabia served until 628. Persian Yemen ends as Persia itself falls apart.

events.title: Death of al-Aʿshā
events.dateNote: Given only as 'shortly before 630'.
events.summary: The poet who alluded to Dhū Qār under the name of the battle of Hinw, and who composed a poem honouring Muḥammad, died not long before 630.
events.dispute: His name, tribe and dates beyond 'died shortly before 630' could not be retrieved. He credited a jinnī named Misḥal with inspiring his poetry.

sources.title: Al-A'sha
sources.note: Gives his death as c. 625, at the low end of this entry's 625–630 range, and has him turned back on the road to Muḥammad.
sources.noteAr: يجعل وفاته نحو 625، وهو أدنى المدى 625–630 في هذا المدخل، ويذكر أنه رجع وهو في طريقه إلى النبي.

sources.title: أعشى قيس
sources.note: Lived into Islam without converting; born and died at Manfūḥa in al-Yamāma.
sources.noteAr: أدرك الإسلام ولم يُسلم، ومولده ووفاته في منفوحة باليمامة.

events.title: Al-Khansāʾ comes to Medina
events.dateNote: Counted in the Hijrī era from 622.
events.summary: She came with a deputation from her clan and embraced Islam. Muḥammad asked her to recite and told her to go on, and is said to have rated her above Imruʾ al-Qays.

events.title: Allāt's shrine at al-Ṭāʾif pulled down
events.dateNote: Dated by the Hijrī chronology of the Ṭāʾif settlement, given as 630 or 631.
events.summary: The cubic rock with its building over it, kept by the Banū ʿAttāb of Thaqīf, was demolished as a condition of the tribe's reconciliation. Her precinct had been ground where trees, game and human blood were all off-limits.

events.title: Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma killed at Ḥunayn
events.dateNote: Ḥunayn is dated in the Hijrī era, 8 AH.
events.summary: An old man carried to the field in a litter, who had fought in about a hundred battles and, Abū ʿUbayda says, lost none. He stayed a pagan to the end. Ibn Sallām called him the first poet of the knights.

events.title: Wadd at Dūmat al-Jandal destroyed
events.dateNote: The expedition is dated April 631 in the Hijrī chronology.
events.summary: An expedition in April 631 was sent to break the idol Wadd, kept by the Banū Kalb at the oasis. Wadd is one of the few of these gods with a genuinely deep inscriptional life — temples, amulets, even Levites in his house at Dadan.

events.title: Dhū al-Khalaṣa pulled down
events.dateNote: Dated April-May 632 in the Hijrī chronology.
events.summary: In April or May the white quartz block called the southern Kaʿba was demolished and burned on Muḥammad's orders. Bajīla had kept it and Khathʿam had defended it; blood-revenge had been decided at it by three arrows.
events.dispute: There is no epigraphic evidence for this cult at all. It is attested only in hadith and in Ibn al-Kalbī's catalogue.

events.title: Death of Muḥammad at Medina
events.dateNote: Dated 8 June 632, 11 AH — the pivot the whole Hijrī chronology is counted from, and the one date in his life that is not reckoned off something else.
events.summary: He died at Medina a few months after the farewell pilgrimage, about sixty-one or sixty-two by the traditional reckoning. Within a year the forces that would take al-Ḥīra and reach the Yarmūk were in the field, and the shrine demolitions that close this atlas — Wadd in 631, Dhū al-Khalaṣa in 632 — belong to the last two years of his life.
events.dispute: The year is as firm as the Arabic tradition gets, being the epoch everything after it is counted from. What it is not is externally attested: the contemporary Greek and Syriac notices of the Arab conquests begin a few years later.

events.title: Al-Ḥīra surrenders
events.dateNote: Dated 12 AH in the conquest narratives.
events.summary: The city gave itself up to Khālid ibn al-Walīd in 12 AH. The court that had paid poets, killed poets, administered in Persian and sent embassies to Constantinople was absorbed into something new.

events.title: Yawm al-Ḥanw
events.dateNote: Undated; the year only holds the day's place in Ibn al-Athīr's order, fifth, between Wāridāt and al-Quṣaybāt.
events.summary: A day Bakr won against Taghlib — one of the two days of this war that the English reconstruction does not record at all. Ibn al-Athīr states it plainly and gives it no narrative beyond the outcome. It falls in his order after Wāridāt, where Hammām ibn Murra was killed, and before al-Quṣaybāt.
events.dispute: The English version lists seven days of the Basūs war and does not mention this one or al-Naqiyya, so the count is nine, not seven — while Ibn al-Athīr himself frames the war as 'five great days', meaning his own formal number is five even though he names nine. No location and no date. Al-ʿIqd al-Farīd lists only five days of the war and does not include this one.

sources.title: ذكر مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب
sources.author: Ibn al-Athīr, ed. ʿUmar ʿAbd al-Salām Tadmurī
sources.note: In his summary list of the five great days al-Ḥanw is the third, won by Bakr over Taghlib.
sources.noteAr: في تعداده المُجمَل للأيام الخمسة الكبرى الحِنْوُ ثالثُها، وكان لبكر على تغلب.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Yawm al-Naqiyya
events.dateNote: Undated; the year only holds the day's place in Ibn al-Athīr's order, eighth, between Quḍa and al-Fuṣayl.
events.summary: Another day to Bakr, after the shaving of the forelocks and before al-Fuṣayl — on the losing side of the hinge, like everything that follows Bujayr's killing. Ibn al-Athīr does no more than name it and give the outcome.
events.dispute: Absent from the English reconstruction entirely, as al-Ḥanw is; with the two of them the war has nine named days rather than seven, though Ibn al-Athīr's own framing calls the great days five. Al-ʿIqd al-Farīd's list of five does not include it. No location, no date, no narrative.

sources.title: ذكر مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب
sources.author: Ibn al-Athīr, ed. ʿUmar ʿAbd al-Salām Tadmurī
sources.note: Names al-Naqiyya among the lesser days after al-Taḥāluq, won by Bakr over Taghlib.
sources.noteAr: يذكر النَّقِيّة في الأيام التي دون الخمسة بعد التحالق، وكانت لبكر على تغلب.

sources.title: مقتل كليب والأيام بين بكر وتغلب (حرب البسوس)

events.title: Palmyrene troops at al-Ḥīra
events.dateNote: The Arabic sources give 132 CE as the oldest documented mention of al-Ḥīra, from a stationing of Palmyrene forces there; the English sources do not carry it and begin with the 4th century.
events.summary: The earliest documented mention of al-Ḥīra: Palmyrene troops stationed at the place, nearly two centuries before the Lakhmid kings make it a capital. The desert-edge site was already worth garrisoning when Palmyra, not Ctesiphon, was the power reaching into the Euphrates steppe.
events.dispute: Outside the file's 300–640 window, so it is reachable by search rather than by the year slider. The English reconstruction does not mention this date at all and starts al-Ḥīra's history in the late 4th century, where Encyclopaedia Iranica puts the arrival of the Lakhm shaykhs; the Arabic sources supply 132 as the oldest documented reference. Nothing connects the garrison to the later Arab city except the place.

sources.title: الحيرة
sources.note: Gives the oldest mention of al-Ḥīra as a text of the Palmyrene era dated 32 CE — not 132 — and says nothing of troops stationed there. The event's year and its garrison claim are not carried by any source found in the 2026-10-19 audit.
sources.noteAr: تجعل أقدمَ ذكرٍ للحيرة نصًّا من زمن مملكة تدمر مؤرَّخًا بعام 32م — لا 132 — ولا تذكر قوّاتٍ مُرابطة فيها. فسنةُ الحدث وخبرُ الحامية لم يحملهما أيُّ مصدرٍ وُجد في مراجعة 19 أكتوبر 2026.

sources.title: Al-Hira
sources.note: Same as the Arabic article: "a Roman source dated to 32 CE mentions a settlement that may correspond to Al-Hira"; no garrison.
sources.noteAr: كالمقالة العربية: مصدرٌ رومانيٌّ مؤرَّخ بعام 32م يذكر مستوطَنةً قد تكون الحيرة؛ ولا ذكرَ لحامية.

people.name: Imruʾ al-Qays
people.lifeNote: Three sets of dates, not two, and no one of them is free of an objection. The Arabic sources give 496–544. The English sources give c. 496 – 565 and c. 526 – 565, and state outright that historians are divided. The Arabic figure of 544 for the death removes the embassy to Caesar of 561–565 altogether, since it would put him seventeen years in the grave before it; c. 496 – 565 makes a man of sixty-three or sixty-four cross the world on a diplomatic journey; c. 526 – 565 makes him an infant when his father was killed c. 525, which cannot be squared with an adult vengeance quest. Present the three as a standing conflict; do not pick one in silence. No inscriptional or external attestation exists for the poet's existence or his dates at all, and he is not the Imruʾ al-Qays of the Namāra inscription of 328.
people.blurb: A dispossessed Kindite prince called the Errant King because he never got his father's throne back. His father Ḥujr took the tribute from the Banū Asad harshly, drove them out when they refused it, and was killed by stealth; the son swore off wine and ornament until he had his revenge, was offered a noble's life or a blood-price in sheep and camels or war, and chose war. He lost his allies when Bakr and Taghlib decided the revenge was enough, hid in a Jewish lord's fortress at al-Ablaq and left three pledges there — his daughter Hind, his cousin and his mail — and never took them back. He rode north with a letter of introduction and died in Anatolia of a skin disease he had already written about in his own verse. The first great poet in Arabic.

path.what: Learns the Banū Asad have killed his father Ḥujr
Fights the vengeance war with Bakr and Taghlib, who then desert him
Takes refuge with al-Samawʾal at al-Ablaq and leaves his daughter, his cousin and his armour in trust
Passes through Ghassanid territory with a letter of introduction
Reaches Justinian and comes away with promises
Falls ill on the road home and dies

people.name: Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd
people.lifeNote: Both dates are reconstructions, giving him about twenty-six years. Nothing independent fixes either.
people.blurb: A young poet at al-Ḥīra who mocked the king and was sent home carrying a sealed letter ordering his own death. His uncle had his read by a boy and threw it in a stream; Ṭarafa would not break a royal seal and carried his to the governor of Baḥrayn. One of the Muʿallaqāt is his.

path.what: At ʿAmr ibn Hind's court, companion of the king's brother
Delivers his own death warrant unopened and is executed

people.name: Al-Mutalammis
people.lifeNote: No dates in any accessible source. He exists in the record almost entirely as the other half of Ṭarafa's story.
people.blurb: Ṭarafa's uncle, and the one who had the sense to get his sealed letter read by a boy from the city before he had walked far enough to be caught. He threw it in the stream and lived.

path.what: Has his death warrant read aloud and destroys it

people.name: ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm
people.lifeNote: No dates found beyond the floruit implied by ʿAmr ibn Hind's reign, 554–568/9. The death year here is a placeholder, not an estimate.
people.blurb: Chief of Taghlib and the author of a Muʿallaqa. The king insulted his mother at dinner and he killed the king for it, which is the single most direct piece of violence any Arabic poet is credited with. His verse is also the only reason anybody remembers Yawm Khazāz.

path.what: Kills ʿAmr ibn Hind at his own table and rides out

people.name: Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza
people.lifeNote: His dates are nowhere given. The only anchor is that his ode addresses ʿAmr ibn Hind, which puts him in 554–568/9.
people.blurb: A Bakrī chieftain whose Muʿallaqa is a legal brief in verse, addressed to the Lakhmid king against Taghlib. Its presence in the canon may owe something to the anthologist's own Bakr patrons.

path.what: Delivers his ode before ʿAmr ibn Hind

people.name: Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā
people.lifeNote: Contradictory inside a single Arabic page: born c. 520 in Najd and died c. 608 in one place, born c. 530 and died between 611 and 627 a few lines further on. Nöldeke gives only 'productive at the end of the 6th century'. The tribe is settled in the Arabic sources — Muzayna, with Murra of the Ḥijāz on his father's mother's side — and he was raised among Ghaṭafān in the house of his maternal uncle Bashāma ibn al-Ghadīr.
people.blurb: The moralist of the Muʿallaqāt, whose closing gnomic lines are the most quoted wisdom verse of the age. His ode was composed after the Dāḥis war ran itself out, and it praises Harim ibn Sinān and al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf by name for paying the blood-money of both sides — about three thousand camels — out of their own property. Harim swore to give him something every time he greeted him, until the poet grew ashamed of what he was taking and would wish a gathering good morning man by man, leaving Harim out. His son Kaʿb later praised Muḥammad. Beware the name-collision with Qays ibn Zuhayr, a different man entirely.

people.name: ʿAntara ibn Shaddād
people.lifeNote: Traditional and reconstructed, not documented, and unstable inside a single Arabic article: the lead gives 608 for the death, the death section gives a life of 525–615, al-Ziriklī gives 600, the text says he reached about ninety and the table says eighty-three. The birth is placed in the first quarter of the 6th century and fixed at 525 from his part in the Dāḥis fighting — so the date is extracted from the battle rather than the battle from the date. Nöldeke places his productive period at the end of the 6th century, which fits the feuds his ode alludes to but sits badly with a 525 birth. The epic's requirement that he fetch a thousand she-camels from al-Nuʿmān III (r. 580–602) is chronologically impossible against that birth date, which is one reason the ʿAbla material belongs to the popular romance layer and not to the old akhbār. His killer is Zurr ibn Jābir al-Nabhānī, not the 'Wasr ibn Jābir' of the English sources.
people.blurb: Son of a free ʿAbsī warrior and an enslaved Ethiopian woman named Zabība, with two enslaved half-brothers, Jarīr and Shaybūb. He was born a slave because the Arabs did not acknowledge the sons of slave women unless they distinguished themselves in war or in poetry — the Arabic sources state that mechanism outright, and it is how he came to be attached to his father's line. One of the three 'crows of the Arabs'. The historical man is a hard-edged boast-and-battle poet with a small dīwān, firmly attested in only two places: the elegy for Mālik ibn Zuhayr and his courage at Dhāt al-Jarājir. The ʿAbsī horseman named at al-Habāʾa is his father Shaddād on the mare Jarwa, not him. The chivalric hero of the ʿAbla romance is a vastly later epic grown by oral accretion from about the twelfth century.

path.what: Composes the elegy for Mālik ibn Zuhayr
Singled out for courage at Yawm Dhāt al-Jarājir
Dies at Ḥāʾil, by the account that lets him reach old age

people.name: Labīd ibn Rabīʿa
people.lifeNote: c. 560 to c. 661 is the conventional range and implies an extreme lifespan. Both figures are conjectural.
people.blurb: The only one of the Muʿallaqāt poets still alive when Muḥammad began preaching, and he converted. He had elegised a Lakhmid king earlier; later a governor of Kūfa sent him a hundred camels so he could keep a vow to feed people whenever the east wind blew.

path.what: Composes an elegy for a Lakhmid king
Comes to Medina and accepts Islam

people.name: Al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī
people.lifeNote: c. 535 to c. 604, both conjectural, the death explicitly called uncertain.
people.blurb: Real name Ziyād ibn Muʿāwiya. The one poet attested shuttling between both client courts: verses about the Lakhmid queen forced him to flee to the Ghassanids, and he came back around 600, then withdrew to his tribe when his patron fell. Al-Mufaḍḍal and Abū ʿUbayda reportedly put his ode among the Seven in place of ʿAntara's and al-Ḥārith's.

path.what: At al-Nuʿmān III's court
In exile with the Ghassanids after offending the king
Returns to al-Ḥīra

people.name: Al-Aʿshā
people.lifeNote: Only 'died not long before 630' is sourced. His name and tribe, conventionally Maymūn ibn Qays of Bakr, could not be confirmed.
people.blurb: He credited a jinnī named Misḥal with his poetry, sang the day of Dhū Qār under another name, and ended up composing a poem in honour of Muḥammad. Sometimes added to the Muʿallaqāt.

people.name: Al-Khansāʾ
people.lifeNote: No birth or death date exists in any accessible source. Her life is pinned only by three events: her brothers' deaths in 612–613, her conversion in 629, and her four sons killed at Qādisiyya in 636.
people.blurb: Tumāḍir bint ʿAmr, 'the snub-nosed', daughter of a clan head. Over a hundred elegies for two dead brothers, nearly a thousand surviving lines of short despairing verse that raised the lament to the standing of high poetry. Her elegies were collected two centuries after her by Ibn al-Sikkīt.

path.what: Her brother Muʿāwiya is killed; Ṣakhr avenges him and dies of his wounds
Comes to Medina with her clan's deputation and converts

people.name: Al-Muhalhil
people.lifeNote: Entirely undated. Even his identification with ʿAdī ibn Rabīʿa, standard in Arabic literature, could not be confirmed from the accessible sources, which name him only as Abū Laylā al-Muhalhil.
people.blurb: Kulayb's brother, Taghlib's war-leader and poet, who swore off perfume and wine until he had killed a man of Bakr for every limb of his brother's body. He won every great day until he killed the young man who came to him with a peace letter, and lost every one after. He ended in Yemen, married into Madhḥij, and died of thirst in a captor's hands.

path.what: Leads Taghlib at al-Nahy
Wins the war's greatest encounter
Composes an elegy over Hammām ibn Murra's body
Taken prisoner at Quḍa and released without being recognised
Settles in Yemen among Janb of Madhḥij
Dies of thirst in captivity near Hajar

people.name: ʿAdī ibn Zayd
people.lifeNote: Born c. 550, died c. 600; both approximate but tied to a documented 579 embassy and a reign, so better anchored than most.
people.blurb: The best insider in the whole period: born at al-Ḥīra into an ʿIbādī Christian family whose grandfather and father had both served the Lakhmids, schooled at the Persian court, speaking Arabic and Persian and probably Syriac, serving as secretary for Arab affairs under two Sasanian kings, sent to Constantinople in 579 and bringing back books. He married into the royal house, helped put his king on the throne, and was imprisoned and strangled by him.

path.what: Educated at the Sasanian court at al-Madāʾin
Goes as a Sasanian envoy and returns with books
Chief councillor to al-Nuʿmān III
Imprisoned and strangled

people.name: Al-Shanfarā
people.lifeNote: No dates whatsoever in the accessible sources; mid-to-late 6th century is a handbook convention nobody could cite, and the c. 525 death figure circulates without apparatus. His tribe, conventionally Azd or Banū Salāmān, is likewise unsourced.
people.blurb: An outlaw poet of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran's band, famous as a runner. He had vowed a hundred Azdī dead and got to ninety-nine; an Azdī who later kicked his skull took a splinter and died of it, which the tradition counts as the hundredth. The Lāmiyyat al-ʿArab that made him famous has been credited since medieval times to a known 8th-century forger.

people.name: Taʾabbaṭa Sharran
people.lifeNote: His dates are explicitly unknown; late 6th or early 7th century is inferred from personal names in the poems.
people.blurb: Thābit ibn Jābir, 'he who carried evil under his arm' — a nickname with three mutually exclusive explanations, one of them that he carried off a ram that turned out to be a ghūl. Unusually for a ṣuʿlūk his own tribe never disowned him. He led a band out of the Sarawāt mountains against Bajīla, Hudhayl, Azd and Khathʿam, and was killed on a raid and thrown into a cave.

path.what: Raiding out of the Sarawāt with his band
Killed raiding Banū Hudhayl; his body thrown into the cave of al-Rakhmān

people.name: ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward
people.lifeNote: 520–600 is given with nothing behind either figure.
people.blurb: The outlaw who stole to feed the poor and was called the most generous of the ancient Arabs. Some of his verse is about the wife he divorced while drunk and could not get back when sober.

people.name: Al-Samawʾal ibn ʿĀdiyāʾ
people.lifeNote: Born early 6th century at Taymāʾ, died c. 560; both reconstructed. His genealogy is disputed — Ibn Durayd makes him a priest's son, al-Jawālīqī gives him a Ghassanid mother and an Azdī father. Whether Imruʾ al-Qays was alive or dead at the time of the siege is unknown.
people.blurb: A Jewish lord of Taymāʾ whose grandfather built the piebald fortress of al-Ablaq on a hill above the Syrian road. He took in Imruʾ al-Qays and kept his deposits, and when a besieger captured his son coming back from a hunt and offered him the choice, he let the boy be killed in front of him rather than hand the property over. 'More faithful than al-Samawʾal' outlived everything else about him.

path.what: Takes in Imruʾ al-Qays and accepts his three deposits
Watches his son killed rather than surrender the trust
Dies at Taymāʾ

people.name: Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿAmr
people.lifeNote: The only pre-Islamic Arab ruler whose death is fixed by a dated inscription: 7 Kaslūl, year 223 of the Bosra era.
people.blurb: Called king of all the Arabs on his own funerary stone. He broke the Asad, drove Madhḥij to the gates of Najrān, subdued Maʿadd and set nobles over them who then served Rome as phylarchs — which makes the 4th-century Lakhmid line Roman-facing, not Persian-facing. Not the poet.

path.what: Buried under the inscription that fixes the century

people.name: Al-Mundhir III ibn al-Nuʿmān
people.lifeNote: Reign 503 or 505 to 554, with the death at Ḥalīma externally dated to June 554. The first Lakhmid who is genuinely historical year by year.
people.blurb: Fifty years of raiding from the Euphrates to Egypt and down into Najd, two Roman commanders captured, Syria burned twice, four hundred nuns reportedly brought home and sacrificed, a victory over Belisarius at Callinicum, and a death on a field in northern Syria at the hands of the Ghassanid he had fought all his life. Anything before him in the Lakhmid list is free narrative space.

path.what: Raids Palaestina Salutaris and Arabia Petraea
Reaches Apamea, fails at Antioch, comes home with plunder
Helps beat Belisarius
Falls at Yawm Ḥalīma

people.name: ʿAmr ibn Hind
people.lifeNote: Reign 554–569 or 570, with the killing given as 568/9 or 569/70. Ry 506 has him acting in 552, two years before the conventional accession, possibly as his father's deputy.
people.blurb: Named after his Kindite mother, and remembered for a violent, implacable temper. He hosted the best poets of his generation, executed one of them by sealed letter, received a Ḥimyarite heir and sent him on to Khusraw, and was killed at his own dinner table by another of his poets over an insult to the man's mother.

path.what: Submits to Abraha and gives up his own son as hostage
Patron of Ṭarafa, al-Mutalammis, al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza and ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm
Killed at dinner

people.name: Al-Mundhir IV
people.lifeNote: Reign given as 574 or 575 to 580 in the conventional table, which is a late reconstruction and unverifiable.
people.blurb: A short-reigning Lakhmid who matters mainly because his name appears among the leaders at Shiʿb Jabala — which is the one detail that makes Caskel's c. 580 date for that battle work and all the others fail.

people.name: Al-Nuʿmān III ibn al-Mundhir
people.lifeNote: Accession given as both 580 and 582 inside a single reference article, and the reign end as 595 in one passage and 602 in another. The 602 fall is externally fixed.
people.blurb: The last Lakhmid king, and the first of his line to convert openly to Nestorian Christianity. He sheltered Khusraw II when the man was a fugitive and fought beside him, then had his own chief councillor strangled, and twelve years later the king he had saved deposed him, seized him at Ctesiphon and left him to die of plague in a prison in the hills. His fall is the hinge of the whole period.

path.what: Shelters the fugitive Khusraw II and fights beside him
Has ʿAdī ibn Zayd imprisoned and strangled
Seized at Ctesiphon after being deposed
Imprisoned at Khānaqīn, where he dies of plague

people.name: Iyās ibn Qabīṣa al-Ṭāʾī
people.lifeNote: Held al-Ḥīra from 602 to 617/18 alongside a Persian co-governor, per the conventional table.
people.blurb: The man Khusraw gave al-Ḥīra to after destroying its dynasty. He had already been made governor of the area, and he is on the Persian side at Dhū Qār — an Arab chief administering an Arab city for an empire whose grip was about to fail.

path.what: Given al-Ḥīra after the dynasty ends
On the Sasanian side when Bakr ibn Wāʾil wins

people.name: Jabalah IV ibn al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Reign 512–529 in the conventional table; the death at Thannuris is externally dated 528, and Simeon's letter puts his camp at al-Jābiya around 520 — an unusually solid early anchor.
people.blurb: A Ghassanid king whose capital was a tent camp between the Ḥawrān and the Golan, and who died fighting the Persians in upper Mesopotamia.

path.what: His camp at al-Jābiya is described in a Syriac letter
Killed at Thannuris

people.name: Al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala
people.lifeNote: Reign c. 528 or 529 to 569; the discrepancy sits between two reference articles. Externally attested throughout by Procopius, Malalas and others.
people.blurb: Greek Arethas. Justinian made him a king and a patrikios and put all Byzantium's Arab allies under him, the highest title ever given a foreign ruler. He fought at Callinicum, where one Greek source says he ran and another says he held; raided Assyria with Belisarius; got the empress to appoint the bishop who built the Syriac Orthodox church; killed the Lakhmid king at Ḥalīma and lost his own eldest son doing it; and at ʿAyn Ubāgh loaded two dead sons on a camel with an enemy king's corpse on top.

path.what: Succeeds his father as phylarch
Raised to kingship and patrikios by Justinian
Commands five thousand Arabs; the sources disagree whether he held or fled
Petitions Theodora and gets Jacob Baradaeus appointed
Kills al-Mundhir III at Ḥalīma and loses his son Jabala
Dies, reportedly during an earthquake

people.name: Al-Mundhir ibn al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Reign 569 to c. 581 or 582, with the arrest dated both ways across sources. A late Syriac chronicle says he came home after Maurice fell in 602.
people.blurb: Greek Alamoundaros. His own emperor ordered him assassinated; he found out and broke with the empire, was reconciled three years later at the shrine of St Sergius, sacked al-Ḥīra in the same year, then was arrested over a failed campaign and exiled to Sicily. A Greek inscription at Ruṣāfa still names him on a building he paid for.

path.what: Discovers Justin II's plot and breaks with Byzantium
Reconciled with the empire at Sergiopolis
Sacks the Lakhmid capital
Arrested, then exiled to Sicily

people.name: Al-Nuʿmān VI ibn al-Mundhir
people.lifeNote: Reign 581–583 in the conventional table; the 584 arrest is externally dated.
people.blurb: Arrested by the Byzantines and tried for treason in 584, after which the Ghassanid confederation came apart into its member tribes. Maurice is said to have put it back together two or three years later because the empire could not hold the desert without it.

path.what: Arrested and tried for treason

people.name: Ḥujr Ākil al-Murār
people.lifeNote: The English sources state that no regnal dates exist for him at all and place him in the early-to-mid 5th century only by inference from his Ḥimyarite sponsor's reign. The Arabic sources give dates: installed in 425 by Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr ibn Tubbāʿ, king of Ḥimyar, and reigning 425–458. The 458 here is the end of that reign and is used as the death year; nothing independent confirms it, and he is also said simply to have reigned long and died of old age at Baṭn ʿAqīl.
people.blurb: 'Eater of bitter herbs', set over the Maʿadd tribes in 425 by a Ḥimyarite king. Kinda's kingship begins with him, as a southern crown's delegated instrument for governing nomads, and the Arabic sources run his reign to 458.

people.name: ʿAmr al-Maqṣūr ibn Ḥujr
people.lifeNote: The English sources have nothing but 'probably killed in battle against the Rabīʿa in the late 5th century'. The Arabic sources give the reign as 458–489, which is where the 489 death year comes from. They also spell the epithet al-Manṣūr, not al-Maqṣūr — a disagreement about the pointing of the name itself, not about the man.
people.blurb: Ḥujr's successor in Najd, reigning 458–489 by the Arabic reckoning, rejected by the Rabīʿa tribes and probably killed fighting them. The Arabic sources write his epithet al-Manṣūr where the English ones write al-Maqṣūr.

people.name: Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr
people.lifeNote: The 502 federate treaty and his existence are externally attested; the manner of his death is contested. The Arabic sources add a reign — 489–528 — and a foundation date of 425 for the kingdom he inherited, where the English ones say no regnal dates were found.
people.blurb: The best-known Kindite king and the first to appear in Byzantine sources, holding a Ḥimyarite mandate, a Byzantine federate treaty and a phylarchate in Palestine at once. He converted to Mazdakism under one Persian king and lost al-Ḥīra when the next one restored the Lakhmids. Killed in the Syrian Desert — by the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III or by the Banū Kalb, depending which source you take. His four sons divided his command and ruined it.

people.name: Ḥujr ibn al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Dated purely by inference from the collapse of Kinda's Ḥimyarite sponsor in 525.
people.blurb: Imruʾ al-Qays's father, set as Kindite regent over the Asad and Ghaṭafān and killed when the Asad revolted. Everything in the most famous biography in Arabic poetry starts from his death.

people.name: Shuraḥbīl ibn al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Entirely undated; placed only after his father's death.
people.blurb: One of the four sons who split the Maʿadd command. He marched on his own brother with the outcasts who attached themselves to kings, each side offering a hundred camels for the other's head, and lost. A man owed blood-money speared him and sent the head to his brother, who wept.

path.what: Defeated and killed at Yawm al-Kulāb I

people.name: Salama ibn al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Shuraḥbīl's brother and the winner at al-Kulāb, who then showed remorse over the head delivered to him. Taghlib expelled him afterwards and he took refuge with Bakr ibn Wāʾil.

people.name: Shammar Yuharʿish
people.lifeNote: Conventionally 275–300 from the inscriptional ruler list; the boundaries are soft.
people.blurb: The king who finished unifying South Arabia under Ḥimyar and gave the dynasty its long title.

people.name: Malkīkarib Yuhaʾmin
people.lifeNote: c. 375–400 from the ruler list.
people.blurb: The king under whom Judaism became Ḥimyar's de facto state religion, though legend gives the credit to his son.

people.name: Abū Karib Asʿad
people.lifeNote: c. 390–440 in the ruler list; the figures are reconstructions from inscriptions and not sharp.
people.blurb: Credited by legend as Ḥimyar's first Jewish convert, and attested campaigning into central Arabia and installing Ḥujr over the Maʿadd — the act that creates the kingdom of Kinda.

people.name: Sharaḥbiʾīl Yaʿfar
people.lifeNote: c. 450–465 in the ruler list; his 450 dam repair is inscription-fixed.
people.blurb: The king who rebuilt the Maʾrib dam in 450 after two consecutive years of breaches.

path.what: Rebuilds the dam

people.name: Dhū Nuwās
people.lifeNote: Accession given as 517, 522, and '518 or 522' across two reference articles. The death is 527 in the Arabic sources — which put the reign at 517–527 and say he died 'at the Red Sea' — and 530 in the English ones, so the death year here follows the Arabic figure while the range stays open. His birth is contradicted inside one Arabic article: the lead has him living 468–527 and the sidebar has him born in 450. The Aksumite conquest that killed him is itself spread 525–543.
people.blurb: Yūsuf Asʾar Yathʾar, the last native Ḥimyarite king and a Jew, who put down the revolt at Najrān and had its Christian leaders killed — an event that brought an Ethiopian army across the Red Sea and ended his kingdom and his line. He is said to have ridden his horse into the sea. The Arabic sources put his death in 527, the English ones in 530, and one Arabic article gives his birth as 468 in its lead and 450 in its table.

path.what: Represses the revolt at Najrān
Killed as the Aksumites take the country

people.name: Al-Ḥārith of Najrān
people.lifeNote: The killing is dated 523, in November by one reckoning, and is the best-documented event in all of pre-Islamic Arabia.
people.blurb: Greek Arethas. The leader of Najrān's Christians, killed with some three hundred and forty followers. A Syriac letter written within months, a Syriac book, a hagiography and three Sabaic inscriptions all bear on his death — and the inscriptions, the only contemporary ones, are political texts that barely mention religion.
