people.name: Kāleb / Ella Asbeha
people.lifeNote: His reign is not fixed in the accessible sources; the invasion he ordered is spread 525–543.
people.blurb: The Christian king of Aksum who sent an army across the Red Sea after the Najrān killings, deposed the Ḥimyarite king and installed a viceroy — and then lost control of his own occupation when one army defected to Abraha and a second was beaten.

people.name: Abraha
people.lifeNote: Tenure given as 535 to 560 or 570, but the detailed inscriptions cover only 547 to 559. Robin argues he probably died c. 570, reasoning back from his sons' reigns in the early 570s. The firm epigraphic window is 547–559, not 535–570.
people.blurb: An Ethiopian general who took Yemen off his own king's viceroy, kept two armies sent against him from retaking it, repaired the Maʾrib dam and celebrated with a mass, hosted envoys from Aksum, Byzantium, Persia and the Ghassanids in one room, raided north into Maʿadd four times and took the son of the king of al-Ḥīra as a hostage. Someone later scratched his name off line 4 of his own inscription. The tradition makes him the man who marched elephants on Mecca.

path.what: Commissions the great dam repairs
Hosts a conference of Aksumite, Byzantine, Persian and Ghassanid envoys
Fourth raid on Maʿadd; takes ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir's son hostage
Last dated text of his reign — the record goes dark

people.name: Masrūq ibn Abraha
people.lifeNote: 571–572 in the ruler list, in a window so tight it strains against the 570 Persian conquest.
people.blurb: Abraha's son by a Ḥimyarite noblewoman, and Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan's half-brother. He was killed in battle when the Persians came, and Ethiopian rule in Yemen ended with him.

people.name: Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan
people.lifeNote: Born around 516 at Ṣanʿāʾ, killed between 575 and 578. There is also a chronological problem on the record: he is said to have been helped by the Lakhmid al-Nuʿmān III, whose reign begins after Sayf's death.
people.blurb: A Ḥimyarite heir from a family that had converted to Judaism, whose father Abraha exiled in order to marry his mother. He went begging to Byzantium, which refused because it shared a faith with his half-brother; then to al-Ḥīra; then to Khusraw's own court, where he got his army on condition Yemen became a Persian vassal. He came home a king who owed tribute and was stabbed to death by one of his own Abyssinian servants. The epic that grew around him sends him into the land of the jinn and gets the Aksumites' religion wrong.

path.what: Refused help by Byzantium
Comes to the Lakhmid court seeking a road to Persia
Granted an army by Khusraw I on condition of vassalage
Installed as vassal king
Stabbed to death by a servant

people.name: Wahrīz
people.lifeNote: The 570 conquest is externally dated; his return is given as 575 or 578.
people.blurb: The Sasanian general who took Yemen with a small expedition and at least eight ships, two of them said to have sunk, besieged Ṣanʿāʾ in 570, and came back after the vassal king was murdered with four thousand men to rule it himself.

path.what: Besieges Ṣanʿāʾ and ends Ethiopian rule
Returns with four thousand men and governs

people.name: Bādhān
people.lifeNote: Served until 628.
people.blurb: The last Sasanian governor of Yemen, unrelated to Wahrīz's family, in post as the empire that appointed him fell apart.

people.name: Khusraw I Anūshirwān
people.lifeNote: Reign 531–579, externally fixed.
people.blurb: He took the throne and immediately bought peace for eleven thousand pounds of Byzantine gold, took Dara after a four-month siege, invaded Anatolia and was beaten near Melitene, sent an army to take Yemen off the Ethiopians, and died with a peace half-negotiated. He reportedly barred future Persian kings from leading armies in person except against another monarch.

people.name: Khusraw II Parvīz
people.lifeNote: Reign 590–628, externally fixed.
people.blurb: He fled his own throne as a young man and was sheltered by the Lakhmid king, and twelve years later destroyed him and his dynasty, clearing the southern flank before declaring the war that took Jerusalem, Egypt and the True Cross — and then lost everything and was killed by his own son.

path.what: Sheltered by al-Nuʿmān III in flight from Bahrām Chōbīn
Deposes and seizes al-Nuʿmān III, ending the Lakhmid kingdom
His armies take Jerusalem and the True Cross
Overthrown and killed

people.name: Justinian I
people.lifeNote: Reign 527–565, externally fixed.
people.blurb: The emperor who made one Arab king answer for the whole eastern frontier, paid for a Perpetual Peace that lasted eight years, and — in the story Arabs told afterwards — received a dispossessed poet-prince and sent him home with a poisoned robe.

people.name: Theodora
people.lifeNote: Died 548.
people.blurb: The empress an Arab Miaphysite king petitioned in 542, and who answered by appointing the bishop who went on to build what became the Syriac Orthodox church.

people.name: Jacob Baradaeus
people.lifeNote: Appointed 542.
people.blurb: Appointed bishop at a Ghassanid king's request, and the man who turned Miaphysite Syria into a church with its own hierarchy. The most consequential thing any Arab client ever caused.

people.name: Justin II
people.blurb: He stopped paying Persia tribute, started a twenty-year war, and ordered his own best Arab ally assassinated.

people.name: Maurice
people.lifeNote: Reign 582–602, murdered.
people.blurb: He exiled one Arab client king to Sicily, broke up the other's confederation, restored a Persian king to his throne — and was murdered by Phocas in 602, which gave that same Persian king his pretext for the final war.

people.name: Phocas
people.blurb: A usurper whose murder of his predecessor handed Khusraw II a casus belli, in the same year Khusraw destroyed the Lakhmids.

people.name: Heraclius
people.blurb: He left Constantinople on 4 April 622 — within weeks of the Hijra — and over six years broke Persia completely, which left both empires too exhausted to hold the desert frontier they had just dismantled.

path.what: Leaves to begin the counteroffensive
Beats Khusraw's army at Ganzaka with Arab help
Breaks the Persian army at Nineveh

people.name: Hind bint al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Undated. The Lakhmid women called Hind are repeatedly conflated in the tradition, and the sources call one of them both daughter and granddaughter of al-Nuʿmān.
people.blurb: A Kindite princess married to the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III and mother of ʿAmr ibn Hind. She converted to Christianity and founded a monastery in the capital; her husband never converted.

people.name: Kulayb ibn Rabīʿa
people.lifeNote: The 494 death comes from one modern Arabic compilation and nothing else. The whole war it starts is now read as a composite of separate raid-stories.
people.blurb: Really named Wāʾil, and called 'little dog' because he staked a puppy at the pastures he reserved for himself and killed anything that came near. He enforced his pasture and water so violently that other tribes came to loathe him. He shot a she-camel that had strayed among his brother-in-law's herd and was speared for it, and forty years of war followed.

people.name: Jassās ibn Murra
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: He speared Kulayb over a camel and his father refused to hand him over, which is the formal start of the war. He raised Kulayb's son himself, and the boy killed him when he found out who his father's killer was.

people.name: Al-Basūs
people.lifeNote: Her name and lineage — al-Basūs bint Munqidh al-Tamīmiyya — appear in Ibn al-Athīr; another account gives her no lineage and only calls her a woman related to Jassās.
people.blurb: The woman whose lament for a killed she-camel went round the camps and made a man kill his brother-in-law. Whether the camel was hers or a guest's, and whether it had a name, depends entirely which source you read.

people.name: Jalīla bint Murra
people.lifeNote: Undated, and absent from several of the sources that cover the war.
people.blurb: Jassās's sister and Kulayb's wife, caught exactly between brother and husband. She had been boasting about her two brothers, which is given as part of why Kulayb was already angry. At the funeral Kulayb's sister reviled her in front of everyone. She went back to her father's house, and the son she bore Kulayb grew up to kill her brother.

people.name: Hammām ibn Murra
people.lifeNote: Undated, and the sources place his death at three different days — Wāridāt, al-Quṣaybāt or Quḍa.
people.blurb: Jassās's brother, and al-Muhalhil's drinking companion before the war — he was the man who carried the news of Kulayb's death to Kulayb's brother. He was killed by a Taghlibī he had fostered himself, and al-Muhalhil composed an elegy over his body.

people.name: Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿUbād
people.lifeNote: Undated. He is absent from every English-language source and recoverable only from the Arabic ayyām chapters.
people.blurb: An old Bakrī champion who sat out the entire war, and came back into it only when the young man he had sent to the enemy with a letter was killed. He shaved his men's heads so they would know each other, cut Taghlib to pieces, took their war-leader prisoner and let him go without recognising him. Whether the dead boy was his son or his nephew, the sources cannot agree.

path.what: Leads Bakr at the shaving of the forelocks and captures al-Muhalhil

people.name: Bujayr
people.lifeNote: Undated. Ibn al-Athīr makes him al-Ḥārith's son, al-Maʿrifa his nephew; one version has him carrying a peace letter, the other an announcement of withdrawal.
people.blurb: The young man sent to the enemy's war-leader, and killed by him. Both versions of the Basūs war turn on his death: Taghlib win every day before it and lose every day after.

people.name: Qays ibn Zuhayr
people.lifeNote: Undated. His appearance as a commander at both Dāḥis and Shiʿb Jabala is a useful relative anchor: it puts the two episodes inside one man's fighting life.
people.blurb: Chief of ʿAbs, who matched his horse against a Dhubyānī's over a course run across forty nights and was cheated of it. He killed the son who came to collect the stake, refused mercy at the well of al-Habāʾa when a man begged him by God and by kinship, and answered the dying with a taunt. At Shiʿb Jabala he kept his camels from water so they would charge toward it. One account has him ending as a hermit in Oman.

path.what: Cheated in the horse race that starts the war
Refuses mercy at the well and has Ḥudhayfa killed
Commands ʿAbs at Shiʿb Jabala
By one account, a hermit in Oman, killed there

people.name: Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Chief of Dhubyān, who won the race by cheating and refused to pay when he lost the argument. At al-Habāʾa the heat got into his thighs and he fell back to the water, which is where they caught him. His last words were a curse that Ghaṭafān would never be reconciled, and his body was mutilated in the way the sources say he had done to boys earlier.

path.what: Wins the rigged race and refuses the stake
Taken prisoner at Yawm al-Ghadaq and released
Run down at the well and killed

people.name: Ḥamal ibn Badr
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Ḥudhayfa's brother, who in one version is the man who hid the ambushers along the race course. At al-Habāʾa he asked his men whom they would least like to see coming, they named two, and those two came. He begged by God and by kinship and was refused.

people.name: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Ziyād
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: An ʿAbsī who paid a hundred camels of blood-money out of his own property early in the war, took Ḥudhayfa prisoner once, and was one of the two men Ḥamal least wanted to see at the well.

people.name: Shaddād ibn Muʿāwiya
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: ʿAntara's father, and the named ʿAbsī cavalryman at al-Habāʾa, riding a mare called Jarwa that he praised in verse. He blocked Dhubyān from reaching their horses, which decided the day.

people.name: Qarāwash ibn ʿAmr
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: The man who struck with a broad-bladed spear at al-Habāʾa and broke Ḥudhayfa's spine.

people.name: Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf al-Murrī
people.lifeNote: Undated. The English-language peace accounts credit him alone, but the Arabic sources put his cousin Harim ibn Sinān in the mediation beside him and make the two of them jointly responsible for the blood-money — about three thousand camels over three years — and jointly praised in Zuhayr's Muʿallaqa. Harim's father Sinān ibn Abī Ḥāritha appears on the opposite side of the matter, as the failed coalition-builder.
people.blurb: The Murrī who cooled the war down, and one of the two men who paid for its end. With his cousin Harim ibn Sinān he covered the blood-price of the dead on both sides out of their own herds and stopped forty years of killing between ʿAbs and Dhubyān. Zuhayr's Muʿallaqa names them both — the connection the English sources could not make and the Arabic ones state outright.

people.name: Laqīṭ ibn Zurāra
people.lifeNote: Undated except relative to Raḥraḥān, which the sources put about a year earlier.
people.blurb: He gave protection to the man who had killed a Hawāzin chief, which turned Banū ʿĀmir against him; then his brother was captured and died a prisoner, and he gathered Tamīm, Dhubyān, Asad, Kindite princes and a Lakhmid force to avenge him. He died in the pass at Shiʿb Jabala and took Kindite power in the north down with him.

path.what: Leads the coalition into the pass and is killed

people.name: Zurāra ibn ʿUdus
people.lifeNote: Undated; he is said to have died in the same days as Raḥraḥān.
people.blurb: Chief of Banū Dārim, warned by a woman who had seen the armies and could tell him who the commanders were — the one warning in the whole corpus that was actually heeded. He got his family and herds away, but his son Maʿbad was taken and died in captivity.

people.name: Maʿbad ibn Zurāra
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Captured by Banū ʿĀmir at Raḥraḥān and kept until he died of it. The captive son dying in enemy hands is the day's whole dramatic residue and the reason for everything that follows.

people.name: Al-Aḥwaṣ ibn Jaʿfar
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Brother of the chief whose killing set the Najd chain in motion, and the man who led the final cavalry charge at Shiʿb Jabala.

people.name: Abū Barāʾ ʿĀmir ibn Mālik
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Called Mulāʿib al-Asinna, the player with spear-points. He led the ʿĀmir and Hawāzin side in the Fijār, and at al-Sullān he knocked an old man down again and again and then asked him to point out someone worth ransoming — and got pointed at a thin black man he took for a slave, who turned out to be worth four hundred camels.

people.name: Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr al-Ḍabbī
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: An old man who forbade his own men to flee at al-Sullān and held the command with his sons standing over him. And then had the presence of mind, flat on his back, to send his attacker after the richest prisoner on the field disguised as a slave.

people.name: Wabra ibn Rūmānis al-Kalbī
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Al-Nuʿmān's half-brother and the commander of his army at al-Sullān, captured in his own charge and ransomed for a thousand camels and a horse, which made his captor rich.

people.name: Ḥanẓala ibn Thaʿlaba al-ʿIjlī
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: One of the Bakrī leaders at Dhū Qār — in a battle where, Landau-Tasseron notes, the leadership shifted from warrior to warrior with no commander-in-chief at all.

people.name: Bisṭām ibn Qays
people.lifeNote: Undated; known from a chapter heading with no narrative recovered.
people.blurb: A famous raider whose death gave a fighting day its name.

people.name: Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī
people.lifeNote: The 578 death comes from Kitāb al-Aghānī alone; another tradition puts it in the year of Muḥammad's birth. No birth date exists anywhere.
people.blurb: A chief of Ṭayyiʾ who is said to have given away everything but his mount and his weapons, associated with the Lakhmid court, and still invoked by name in a living proverb. The riddle-quest romances built on him in Persian and Urdu are centuries later.

people.name: Al-Barrāḍ ibn Qays
people.lifeNote: Undated except through the Fijār's own loose window.
people.blurb: A man his own tribe had expelled, who killed a Banū ʿĀmir notable during a sacred month and seized a king's caravan. The sacrilege that gave the Fijār wars their name.

people.name: ʿUrwa al-Raḥḥāl
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Killed in a sacred month while escorting the Lakhmid king's caravan, which set four years of fighting going at the fairground.

people.name: Qays ibn ʿĀṣim
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Led the Madhḥij side at al-Kulāb II, in a fight his people's elders had advised against and the other side had been pushed into by a soothsayer.

people.name: Ḥuḍayr al-Katāʾib
people.lifeNote: Dated only by Buʿāth's position before the Hijra.
people.blurb: The Aws commander at Buʿāth. His side was losing until he reminded them out loud of every wrong the Khazraj had ever done them, and they turned it around.

path.what: Rallies the Aws and wins the day

people.name: ʿAmr ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Bayāḍī
people.lifeNote: Dated only by Buʿāth.
people.blurb: The Khazraj chief who took hostages from the Jewish tribes of the oasis and killed them when they would not hand over property — and so drove those tribes into the other side's camp. He was killed in the fighting that followed.

people.name: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy
people.lifeNote: Chosen as peace-keeper after Buʿāth, c. 617; lost influence after 622.
people.blurb: Chosen by both exhausted tribes to keep the peace at Yathrib after Buʿāth. The consensus leader of a post-civil-war oasis — and the vacancy his weakness left is the one Muḥammad walked into in 622.

people.name: Qusayy ibn Kilāb
people.lifeNote: The sharpest chronological contradiction in the whole record: Hawting says his children must have lived in the second half of the fifth century, Watt says Qusayy himself probably died in the second half of the sixth. A hundred years apart, unresolved.
people.blurb: The man who pulled the scattered descendants of Fihr together, took the Meccan sanctuary and set up the clan offices everything after him runs on. The name Quraysh may come from him.

people.name: Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma
people.lifeNote: Died January 630. His birth is given only as the 6th century.
people.blurb: Chief of Banū Jusham, who fought in about a hundred battles and, one authority says, lost none. He stayed a pagan into extreme old age and was carried to his last battle in a litter. Called the first poet of the knights.

people.name: Musaylima
people.lifeNote: His claim is placed before the Hijra, c. 622; nothing else is fixed.
people.blurb: A soothsayer of the settled farming Yamāma who declared himself a prophet in his own village before the Hijra. Central Arabia produced its own claimants.

people.name: Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī
people.lifeNote: Considered legendary or semi-legendary and known only from Muslim sources. His lifespan is given as 380, 600 or 700 years, which is as clear a marker of accretion as the corpus offers.
people.blurb: He stood up in the market at ʿUkāẓ and preached one God and the resurrection in rhymed prose, and tradition puts the young Muḥammad in the audience. Called a bishop of Najrān in some accounts and a pagan sage in others. One sermon survives.

path.what: Preaching at the fair

people.name: Zarqāʾ al-Yamāma
people.lifeNote: Entirely legendary, and her story's sourcing is weak — a comparative-literature book and a newspaper feature. Her sight-range is given as a week, not the three days usually repeated.
people.blurb: The blue-eyed woman who could see riders a week away. The enemy came hidden behind trees they carried, and she said the trees were moving, and her people decided she had gone mad. After they killed the men of the camp the invaders tore out her eyes and crucified her. The most persistent shape in the whole corpus is the woman who warns and is not believed.

people.name: Saṭīḥ
people.lifeNote: Savran reads both Saṭīḥ and Shiqq as early-ʿAbbāsid literary constructions — connectors inserted to tie ancient Arabia, Persia and the rise of Islam into one narrative — not as remembered 6th-century figures. Using them as period characters reproduces an ʿAbbāsid ideology.
people.blurb: A seer with almost no bones in him, compared to a doormat, whom his companions folded up when they travelled. He and his half-bodied companion got their gift from a prophetess who had predicted the Maʾrib dam's collapse. His last prophecy, delivered on his deathbed to a Christian envoy sent from a Persian king, was that Persian rule would pass to the Arabs — and then he died on the spot.

path.what: A Christian of al-Ḥīra is sent to find him with the Persian king's question

people.name: Shiqq
people.lifeNote: Same verdict as for Saṭīḥ: an ʿAbbāsid construction, not a remembered figure. The popular version giving him a jinn mother is not supported by the one specialist source available.
people.blurb: A seer with half a face, half a head and half a body — his name means 'half'. The seer and the half-being are the same image across this whole corpus: the one who sees the unseen is himself not quite a whole man.

people.name: Bilqīs
people.lifeNote: The Qurʾān never names her; the name and the jinn parentage are both exegetical, from al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī. No inscription names any such queen, and the Awwām temple folk-named after her was excavated with nothing linking it to her.
people.blurb: The queen of Sabaʾ, unnamed in scripture, who sent gifts that were refused, came to Solomon's palace and lifted her clothes crossing a floor she took for water. The hairy legs that explain the glass floor are a folk elaboration on an exegetical elaboration — two steps out from a text that says only that she bared her shins.

people.name: Ḥalīma bint al-Ḥārith
people.lifeNote: Undated. The Arabic sources are more precise than the English ones about who she was: a daughter of al-Ḥārith the Ghassanid king himself, and the day is named after her. The proverb usually attached to her — that Ḥalīma's day is no secret — appears in al-Khāqānī's list.
people.blurb: Daughter of al-Ḥārith ibn Jabala, the Ghassanid king, and not merely a princess who helped her tribe's fighters: the Arabic sources make her the king's own daughter and say the day carries her name because of her. The best-dated battle in the whole Arabic corpus is called after her.

people.name: Abū Karib
people.lifeNote: Undated.
people.blurb: Al-Ḥārith's son, who came out for the single combat at ʿAyn Ubāgh and killed the man sent against him — and only then found out it had not been the enemy king's son at all, but a champion in his clothes.

people.name: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ
people.lifeNote: An 8th-century Basran philologist, well outside the period, included because of what he said about it.
people.blurb: He sat in a Friday circle at Baṣra while men argued over who had led the Arabs at Khazāz, and ruled against all three candidates on the grounds that the day was older than any of them — adding that he had been asking the question for sixty years and had never found anybody who knew. The most honest sentence in the entire corpus.

people.name: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh
people.lifeNote: The death is the firm end: 8 June 632, the pivot the whole Hijrī chronology is counted from, and the Hijra of 622 is fixed as that calendar's epoch. The birth is not. Tradition pegs it to the Year of the Elephant, and this atlas dates that event across 552-572, so the birth year inherits a twenty-year spread and the conventional 570 is a synchronism built to anchor it rather than a transmitted date. Everything in his life reckoned by age — the marriage, the rebuilding of the Kaʿba, the age of forty at the first revelation — inherits that spread; everything reckoned in years before the Hijra does not. There is no inscriptional, archaeological or external documentary evidence for Mecca or Quraysh before 632, so the Meccan half of his life rests entirely on the later Arabic biographical tradition, written down about a century and a half after the events.
people.blurb: A Meccan of the Banū Hāshim, posthumous son of ʿAbd Allāh, orphaned young and raised by his grandfather and then his uncle Abū Ṭālib. He married the merchant Khadīja bint Khuwaylid, was known as an arbitrator before he was known as anything else, and from about 610 preached one God, the resurrection and the judgement in a town whose sanctuary held the gods of a whole region's tribes. Boycotted with his clan, bereaved of his wife and his protector in the same year, he sent followers to Christian Aksum, took oaths from men of Yathrib at al-ʿAqaba, and moved to that oasis in 622. He died at Medina in 632, by which time most of the peninsula's tribes had come to terms with him.

path.what: Born at Mecca in the year tradition calls the Year of the Elephant
The revelation begins during a retreat at the cave of Ḥirāʾ
Takes the first pledge from men of Yathrib at al-ʿAqaba
Moves to Yathrib; the Hijra
Dies at Medina

people.name: Khadīja bint Khuwaylid
people.lifeNote: No birth date exists. The tradition makes her about forty at her marriage c. 595 and has her die in the Year of Sorrow, given as 619 or 620. Her standing as a merchant who financed caravans is repeated everywhere in the sīra and interrogated nowhere: the searches for critical scholarship on it turned up only devotional and popular writing.
people.blurb: A Meccan businesswoman of the Banū Asad branch of Quraysh, twice widowed, who employed Muḥammad on a Syrian caravan and then married him. She was his only wife while she lived, and the first to accept what he said he had heard at Ḥirāʾ. Her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, named in the lists of pre-Islamic Arab monotheists, is the man the tradition has her take him to.

people.name: Abū Ṭālib ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib
people.lifeNote: No birth date. His death is placed in the Year of Sorrow, 619 or 620, by its position relative to the Hijra rather than by any record. His floruit, like his father's, is undated in the sources reached.
people.blurb: Head of the Banū Hāshim after ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and guardian of his orphaned nephew. He never accepted his nephew's preaching but extended clan protection over him, which is what made the boycott of the Hāshim necessary and what his death removed. Father of ʿAlī.

people.name: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim
people.lifeNote: His floruit is undated in every source reached. The conventional 578 for his death is arithmetic off a contested birth year: tradition has him die when his grandson was eight, and the grandson's birth is placed anywhere in 552-572. The stories attached to him — Hubal's arrows choosing his son ʿAbd Allāh for sacrifice and a hundred camels offered instead, his dealings with Abraha in the Elephant narrative, the rediscovery of the Zamzam well — are all narrative, and the hundred-camel blood-price often credited to him could not be sourced to him specifically.
people.blurb: Head of the Banū Hāshim, custodian of the sanctuary's water and of his clan's share in the Meccan offices, and the figure through whom the Quraysh genealogies pass. His sons included ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Ṭālib, Ḥamza and al-ʿAbbās. The later name of the Banū Hāshim was simply Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

people.name: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib
people.lifeNote: Known only as his son's father. The tradition has him die on a trading journey about six months before the birth, which makes his death date move with the birth date across 552-572. Al-Zuhrī preserves a tradition that puts the Year of the Elephant before he was even born, which breaks the synchronism from inside the tradition.
people.blurb: A son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, said in the Hubal-arrows story to have been the one chosen for sacrifice and ransomed with a hundred camels. He died young, away from Mecca, leaving a pregnant wife.

people.name: Āmina bint Wahb
people.lifeNote: No dates of her own. Her death is reckoned as her son's sixth year, so it moves with his contested birth year across the whole 552-578 span. Nothing external touches her.
people.blurb: Of the Banū Zuhra of Quraysh, widowed before her son was born and dead while he was a small child. The tradition has her send him out to a wet-nurse among the Banū Saʿd of Hawāzin, which is the ordinary Meccan practice of the time and not a detail about her.

people.name: Al-Najāshī, the Negus of Aksum
people.lifeNote: The Islamic sources give him only a title, not a name that can be matched to the Aksumite king-list. He has been identified with Armah since 1895 and alternatively with Ella Tsaham, and Hahn has argued Armah was a son of Kāleb under another name; the Aksumite coin sequence gives relative order, not absolute dates, so none of the identifications is fixed. The one near-anchor is Munro-Hay's reading of a three-cross reverse as a reference to the Persian capture of Jerusalem in 614, and that reading is itself conditional.
people.blurb: The Christian king of Aksum who, in the sīra, gave asylum to Meccan emigrants and refused a Qurashī delegation's request to send them back. Whoever he was, the episode puts Mecca inside the Red Sea world that Aksum and Ḥimyar had been fighting over for a century.

people.name: Harim ibn Sinān al-Murrī
people.lifeNote: The Arabic sources date his death to about 15 years before the Hijra, that is c. 608 CE, on land of the Banū Asad called Ruzāʾ, while he was on his way to al-Nuʿmān III at al-Ḥīra. That date appears in no English-language source at all. His role in the Dāḥis settlement is firm in the Arabic record — he and his cousin al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf entered the mediation together and carried the blood-money out of their own property, some three thousand camels over three years — which the English reconstruction had marked unverified and warned against building on. The Arabic sources also correct the report that his brother Khārija carried the blood-money: that is not sound. His father Sinān ibn Abī Ḥāritha stands on the opposite side of the matter, as the man who assembled a larger coalition against ʿAbs and then withdrew without fighting; father and son, not a contradiction.
people.blurb: A Dhubyānī nobleman who paid for the end of a forty-year war out of his own herds, together with his cousin al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf: three thousand camels over three years, the blood-price of both sides' dead. Zuhayr praised the two of them in his Muʿallaqa for what they did about the war, and Harim gave him so much for the praise that the poet grew ashamed to take it — he took to greeting a gathering by wishing every man in it good morning except Harim. He died on the road to al-Ḥīra, on Asad land, about 608.

path.what: Enters the Dāḥis mediation with his cousin al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf and pays the blood-money
Dies on Banū Asad land at Ruzāʾ, travelling to al-Nuʿmān III at al-Ḥīra

people.name: Hawdha ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥanafī
people.lifeNote: Undated. He surfaces in the Arabic account of Yawm al-Ṣafqa as Khusraw's man in al-Yamāma, raised in the king's regard after he treated the Persian envoys whom Tamīm had robbed well. A footnote version from Jād al-Mawlā reverses his fortune entirely: Tamīm ambushed and captured him in a valley and would not release him for less than three hundred camels.
people.blurb: Khusraw's agent in al-Yamāma, and the man charged with punishing Tamīm for robbing the king's caravan. He is also the one piece of mercy in the story: the day of the killing fell on Easter, so he asked al-Mukaʿbir for a hundred of the Tamīmī prisoners and set them free, and al-Aʿshā made a poem of it.

path.what: Draws Tamīm to the fortress of al-Mushaqqar, then frees a hundred of them

people.name: Al-Mukaʿbir
people.lifeNote: Undated, and known by a nickname rather than a name. He is the Persian commander sent with a force of asāwira — heavy cavalry — to deal with Tamīm, and the man who closed the gate that gave the day its name.
people.blurb: The Persian officer at al-Mushaqqar. He and Hawdha let the Tamīmīs into the fortress in small parties on a promise of grain in a hard year and killed them group by group; when a man of ʿAbs cut the chain off the door and those at the gate got out, he shut the gates and killed everyone left inside. The day is called al-Ṣafqa, the closing, after what he did with those doors.

path.what: Shuts the gates of al-Mushaqqar on the Banū Tamīm

polities.name: Lakhmids of al-Ḥīra
polities.blurb: Arab kings at the desert edge of Mesopotamia, clients of Persia, holding a Christian city of palaces and monasteries and salaried scribes. Their reach was not a border but a pull: tribes of the lower Euphrates and eastern Arabia answered them, and their raiding parties went as far as Egypt and down into Najd. Khusraw II destroyed them in 602.

polities.name: Ghassanids / Jafnids
polities.blurb: Byzantium's Arab phylarchs in Syria: Miaphysite Christians whose capital was a royal tent camp, whose ceremonial centre was a desert martyr's shrine, and whose king once outranked every other foreign ruler in the empire's protocol. Byzantium broke the confederation in 584 and never fully put it back.

polities.name: Kingdom of Kinda
polities.blurb: A Ḥimyar-sponsored over-tribal power in Najd, set up to govern the Maʿadd nomads on a southern crown's behalf. The Arabic sources date its founding to 425, when Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr ibn Tubbāʿ, king of Ḥimyar, set Ḥujr Ākil al-Murār over the Maʿadd, and give the reigns in order — Ḥujr 425–458, ʿAmr 458–489, al-Ḥārith 489–528 — where the English sources state outright that no regnal dates could be found. It also held a Byzantine federate treaty and a Palestinian phylarchate at the same time, which is probably why it fractured faster than any other buffer power. After the Ethiopian conquest of Ḥimyar in 525 it broke into small kingdoms that fell one after another between 530 and 540 to successive ʿAdnānī raids. Its kings' sons destroyed what was left among themselves.

polities.name: Ḥimyar
polities.blurb: The one Arabian power with a real epigraphic chronology. Kings of Sabaʾ and dhū-Raydān, officially monotheist from about 380 and Judaic for a century and a half after, reaching into central Arabia through clients and into the dam-fed oasis at Maʾrib with public works that needed a state to maintain them.

polities.name: Aksum
polities.blurb: The Christian Ethiopian kingdom across the Red Sea, with a Red Sea port, a navy good enough to move an army, and a claim on South Arabia it made good in the 520s.

polities.name: Aksumite Yemen
polities.blurb: Forty-five years of Ethiopian rule in South Arabia, most of it under a general who had taken the country off his own king's viceroy. Churches went up, the dam was repaired, envoys from four powers met at Maʾrib in one room, and armies went north into Maʿadd four times. Then the epigraphic record stops, and ten years later the Persians arrive.

polities.name: Sasanian Yemen
polities.blurb: Persia took South Arabia with a small expedition and held it for nearly sixty years through vassal kings and then governors. The dam was never repaired again.

polities.name: Sasanian Empire
polities.blurb: The eastern empire, whose southern frontier ran through Arab clients rather than fortifications: the Lakhmids on the Euphrates, a governor in al-Baḥrayn, a province in Oman, a fort on the Omani coast, and from 570 a conquered Yemen.

polities.name: Byzantine Empire
polities.blurb: The western empire, which held the Syrian desert frontier through Arab phylarchs, paid Persia gold to stop fighting four separate times, and then dismantled its own Arab buffer in 584 just before the war that ruined everything.

polities.name: Quraysh of Mecca
polities.blurb: Clans holding a sanctuary town in a dry valley, running winter caravans south to Yemen and summer caravans north to Gaza, Bosra and Damascus, buying estates in the cooler town above them and taking over its trade. There is not one inscription, dig or outside document for them before 632.

polities.name: Yathrib
polities.blurb: Not a city but a spread of fortified farmsteads and palm groves, held by two Arab tribes and three Jewish ones in shifting alliance, and fought over for a century until 617 left both Arab tribes exhausted enough to appoint a single peace-keeper.

polities.name: The Nabataean ruins
polities.blurb: A kingdom that ended in 106 and stayed in the landscape: carved tomb facades at Petra and Hegra, high places on the peaks, betyls in their niches, and a dating era still being used in 568. In the 6th century the tombs at Hegra were read as the houses of a race God destroyed.

polities.name: Sasanian al-Baḥrayn
polities.blurb: The eastern coast under Persian suzerainty and Lakhmid administration, with a scatter of Nestorian bishoprics on the islands and a governor who executed poets on a Lakhmid king's written order.

tribes.name: Bakr ibn Wāʾil
tribes.blurb: A confederation running from south-western Iraq into eastern Arabia, with Shaybān as its strongest branch. Forty years at war with Taghlib over a camel, and then the tribe that beat a Persian column at Dhū Qār and was remembered for it.

tribes.name: Taghlib
tribes.blurb: Kulayb's and al-Muhalhil's people, who won every great day of the Basūs war until their war-leader killed a peace envoy, and lost every one after. Christianised and dispersed into the Jazīra and lower Iraq, which the war-story explains as a defeat and probably is not.

tribes.name: Banū ʿAbs
tribes.blurb: ʿAntara's tribe and Qays ibn Zuhayr's, and the ʿAbs of forty years of killing with Dhubyān over a rigged horse race. Some of them stayed out of it to guard Lakhmid caravans, which is exactly the detail that wrecks the war's traditional dates.

tribes.name: Dhubyān and Fazāra
tribes.blurb: Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr's people, Ghaṭafānī, and ʿAbs's enemies in the long feud. At al-Habāʾa they lost about four hundred men in a morning and called the day the Perdition.

tribes.name: Banū Tamīm
tribes.blurb: A very large tribe across north-eastern Arabia, with Dārim and Yarbūʿ among its branches. It fought nearly everyone — Bakr, ʿĀmir, Madhḥij, the Lakhmids, the Persians at al-Mushaqqar — and much later got accused of female infanticide by its political enemies.

tribes.name: Banū Asad
tribes.blurb: The tribe that killed Ḥujr and so set the most famous vengeance quest in Arabic poetry going. Also the tribe of ʿAbīd ibn al-Abraṣ, a poet and contemporary of the man who came to avenge his father on them.

tribes.name: Ṭayyiʾ
tribes.blurb: The tribe under the twin mountains at Ḥāʾil, Ḥātim's people, with a reputation for generosity built on one man. They also supplied the chief Khusraw handed al-Ḥīra to in 602.

tribes.name: Ghaṭafān
tribes.blurb: The parent grouping over Dhubyān, Fazāra and ʿAbs, so most of the Dāḥis war is internal to it. Ghaṭafān stayed out of the Fijār on the Qays side.

tribes.name: Hawāzin
tribes.blurb: The confederation that won four of the Fijār days against Quraysh and lost only one. Banū ʿĀmir and Thaqīf sit under it, and so does Labīd.

tribes.name: Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa
tribes.blurb: Hawāzin's biggest branch, with Kilāb and Kaʿb and Jaʿfar under it. Victors at Shiʿb Jabala, caravan-robbers at al-Sullān, and a party to half the fighting days of Najd.

tribes.name: Kinda
tribes.blurb: Originally South Arabian and moved north into Najd in the 4th or 5th century, where a Ḥimyarite mandate made its chiefs kings over the nomads. Imruʾ al-Qays's house. After Shiʿb Jabala much of it withdrew to Ḥaḍramawt.

tribes.name: Quraysh
tribes.blurb: The clans of the Meccan sanctuary, split into the Confederates and the Perfumed and into those who lived around the Kaʿba and those on the outskirts. Caravan merchants with alliances bought from the bedouin along the route.

tribes.name: Aws
tribes.blurb: One of the two Arab tribes of Yathrib, allied with the Jewish Qurayẓa and Naḍīr, and the winners at Buʿāth.

tribes.name: Khazraj
tribes.blurb: The other Arab tribe of Yathrib, allied with Qaynuqāʿ. Its chief's killing of Jewish hostages is what pushed the other two Jewish tribes to the opposite side and lost him the day and his life.

tribes.name: Hudhayl
tribes.blurb: A Ḥijāzī tribe in the hills around Mecca, keepers of the idol Suwāʿ, and the people Taʾabbaṭa Sharran spent his life raiding and died raiding.

tribes.name: Banū Ḥanīfa
tribes.blurb: Settled farmers of the Yamāma with date groves and wheat fields, who supplied grain to Mecca and sent skilled workers there. Not nomads at all — and their travellers are the ones recorded asking a valley's jinn for safe passage.

tribes.name: Madhḥij
tribes.blurb: A large southern grouping, driven to the gates of Najrān in the 328 inscription and still fighting Tamīm at al-Kulāb nearly three centuries later. Al-Muhalhil ended his life married into one of its clans.

tribes.name: Azd
tribes.blurb: A southern tribal mass whose dispersal northward the genealogies explain by the Maʾrib dam's failure — a story that puts a 2nd-century ancestor in charge of a 6th-century flood, and does real etiological work explaining why Yemeni-descended tribes are in Syria, Mecca and Medina.

tribes.name: Judhām
tribes.blurb: A tribe of the north-western marches between the Ḥijāz and the Roman frontier, in the orbit of the Byzantine clients.

tribes.name: Banū Kalb
tribes.blurb: The dominant tribe at Dūmat al-Jandal and across the Wādī Sirḥān corridor, keepers of the idol Wadd, and a tribe whose men turn up on both imperial sides — including as a Lakhmid army commander and as a possible killer of a Kindite king.

tribes.name: Iyād
tribes.blurb: A north Arabian tribe in the Lakhmid orbit, present as Persian auxiliaries at Dhū Qār, and the tribe of the preacher who stood up at ʿUkāẓ and spoke about one God.

tribes.name: Quḍāʿa
tribes.blurb: A large northern grouping spanning the Syrian desert margins, with Kalb among its branches, and an opponent of Kinda in the earliest-remembered of the fighting days.

tribes.name: Thaqīf
tribes.blurb: The tribe of al-Ṭāʾif, keepers of Allāt's cubic rock, Mecca's commercial rival and its ally in the Fijār.

tribes.name: Khuzāʿa
tribes.blurb: A Ḥijāzī tribe that held the Meccan sanctuary before Quraysh, and which the tradition blames for importing the idols that stood around the Kaʿba.

tribes.name: Banū Sulaym
tribes.blurb: Al-Khansāʾ's tribe, Hawāzin-side in the Fijār, and the people whose skirmishes with Murra and Asad killed both of her brothers and produced a thousand lines of elegy.

tribes.name: Shaybān
tribes.blurb: Bakr's hardest branch: Jassās's clan, the Basūs war's engine, and the core of the force that beat the Persians at Dhū Qār.
